article-108.title: Diving the Maldives: beyond the resort
article-108.fulltext:
Some journeys change the shape of a year. This is one of them — a route our trip designers return to again and again, refined with the local guides who know every ridge, kitchen and hidden trail.

We build each departure around small groups, vetted partners and the kind of access that turns a holiday into a story. What follows is what to expect, when to go, and how to make it your own.

When to go

Shoulder season brings the best light and the thinnest crowds. Our planners watch the calendar so you do not have to.

What you get

Hand-built itineraries, real humans on call, and partners we have travelled with ourselves. No filler days, no tourist traps — just the good stuff, paced the way you like it.

“The details were handled before we even thought to ask.”

Make it yours

Add a rest day, swap a hike for a cooking class, extend a night under the stars. Every trip is a starting point, not a script.

Shoulder season brings the best light and the thinnest crowds. Our planners watch the calendar so you do not have to.

What you get

Hand-built itineraries, real humans on call, and partners we have travelled with ourselves. No filler days, no tourist traps — just the good stuff, paced the way you like it.

“The details were handled before we even thought to ask.”

Make it yours

Add a rest day, swap a hike for a cooking class, extend a night under the stars. Every trip is a starting point, not a script.

article-200.title: Privacy Policy
article-200.introtext: Voyara respects your privacy. This policy explains what personal data we collect when you use this site, why we collect it, and the choices you have.
article-200.fulltext:
What we collect

When you create an account, subscribe to our newsletter or make an enquiry we collect the details you give us — typically your name, email address and any trip preferences you share. When you browse the site we also collect standard technical data such as your IP address, device type and the pages you view.

How we use your data

  • To create and manage your account and respond to your enquiries.
  • To plan, confirm and support the trips you book with us.
  • To send you travel inspiration and offers, where you have opted in.
  • To keep the site secure and to improve how it works.

Cookies and analytics

We use cookies and similar technologies to keep you signed in, to remember your preferences and to understand how the site is used. You can control cookies through your browser and through the choices described in our Cookie Policy.

Your rights

You can ask us to access, correct or delete the personal data we hold about you, and you can withdraw consent to marketing at any time. We keep your data only for as long as we need it to provide our services or to meet our legal obligations.

Contact

For any question about this policy, or to exercise your rights, write to us at privacy@voyara.example and we will respond promptly.

article-201.title: Booking & cancellation policy
article-201.introtext:
BOOKING TERMS

Booking & cancellation policy

Deposits

A 20% deposit secures your departure. The balance is due 45 days before travel. For trips booked within 45 days of departure, full payment is taken at the time of booking.

Changes & cancellations

Date changes are free up to 60 days before departure, subject to availability. Cancellations are refunded on a sliding scale detailed in your confirmation email.

article-202.title: Cookie Policy
article-202.introtext: This policy explains how Voyara uses cookies and similar technologies, and how you can control them.
article-202.fulltext:
What cookies are

Cookies are small text files a website stores on your device. They let the site remember your actions and preferences over time, so you do not have to re-enter them each time you return.

The cookies we use

  • Essential cookies that keep you signed in and remember items such as your language and theme.
  • Analytics cookies that tell us, in aggregate, which pages are popular so we can improve the site.
  • Marketing cookies, set only with your consent, that help us show relevant travel offers.

Managing cookies

You can accept or reject non-essential cookies when you first visit, and change your mind at any time through your browser settings. Blocking essential cookies may stop parts of the site — such as signing in — from working correctly.

Changes to this policy

We may update this policy as our site evolves or as the law changes. Any material change will be posted here with a revised date, so it is worth checking back from time to time.

article-214.title: Walking the Kungsleden under midnight sun
article-214.introtext: The Kungsleden — the King's Trail — runs for 440 kilometres from Abisko in the north to Hemavan in the south through some of Scandinavia's most remote mountain terrain. I walked the northern hundred kilometres from Abisko to Kebnekaise in early August, when the sun stays above the horizon for twenty-two hours a day and the willow ptarmigans are still raising chicks in the heather beside the trail. The light is the variable that no photograph reproduces: a perpetual amber quality, like standing inside a lantern, that makes the most ordinary stretch of birch forest look like a passage from a book about somewhere else. The Swedish Tourist Association mountain cabins along the route are a civilising influence: self-catering kitchens with gas stoves, simple bunks, and a sauna at every fourth station. At Alesjaure, the cabin manager had been running the hut for eighteen consecutive summers and could identify exactly where each group had come from by the state of their boots.

article-215.title: Acclimatising for Kilimanjaro the slow way
article-215.introtext: Most teams spend six days on Kilimanjaro. Our team spent eight, and that small difference is the reason I reached the summit at 5,895 metres without a headache and with a clear memory of the last hour on the crater rim. Slow acclimatisation is the single variable that changes Kilimanjaro from a slog into an experience, and yet the majority of the agencies at the gate still push the standard six-day packages because the arithmetic works in their favour. The Lemosho route, which starts further west and crosses the Shira Plateau before joining the summit approach, gives you the extra altitude days if you choose the eight-day option and are willing to pay the additional park fees. We climbed at night from Barafu camp with head torches and layered everything we owned. The wind at Stella Point was 50 kilometres per hour and the temperature was minus fifteen. The sunrise on the ice fields, turning from grey to apricot to white gold as the shadow line crossed the crater, made the arithmetic irrelevant.

article-216.title: The W Trek minus the high-season crowds
article-216.introtext: Torres del Paine in October carries two separate reputations: the crowds who arrive in January barely recognise the mountain from the weather window that arrives in late spring, when the queues at the hiker's hot springs are two days long and the campsites resemble weekend festivals. I walked the W Trek in the second week of October to confirm a different rumour: that the shoulder season offers the same granite towers, the same electric-blue glaciers and the same burnt-orange pampas but in a different register of silence. The refuges were thirty percent full. The ferries ran on time. The wind was still formidable — it always is — but the park service staff were willing to sit and talk at length about the changes they have seen in the ice since the eighties. I booked six months ahead and still found premium bunk spots at Chileno and Paine Grande, the two chokepoints on the central circuit.

article-217.title: Nepal Manaslu Circuit teahouse by teahouse
article-217.introtext: The Manaslu Circuit is Nepal's quietest great circuit, taking a ten-day anticlockwise loop around the world's eighth-highest mountain through valleys that have remained off the main trekking circuit despite being on the permit system since 1991. I walked it in mid-October with a single guide and no porter, carrying a pack that weighed fourteen kilograms by the end of the first resupply and eleven by the time we crossed Larkya La at 5,106 metres. The passes are a small industry of permit checking and the teahouses are more variable than on Annapurna: some are run by families who have been in the hospitality business for three generations, some by young entrepreneurs who learned their English from trekkers and are aggressively expanding their charging points and menu lamination. The altitude above four thousand metres is where the circuit earns its reputation. The final approach to the pass involves five hours of darkness broken only by head torches and the sound of ice cracking somewhere higher up the ridge.

article-218.title: Scrambling the Drakensberg amphitheatre
article-218.introtext: The Drakensberg Amphitheatre is a fourteen-kilometre basalt wall that drops a thousand metres from the escarpment to the valley floor in a single unbroken cliff, the longest and highest in the southern hemisphere. I approached it from the north, camping two nights at the base and reaching the Chain Ladder at dawn on the third morning. The chains are fixed into the rock at the two crux points and most hikers treat them as a route-finding aid rather than a safety device, but in wet conditions they are essential: the basalt becomes slick within minutes of rainfall and the drop on the exposed sections is absolute. The summit plateau is a different biome: rolling moorland, scattered sinkholes, and the source of the Tugela River, the second-highest waterfall in the world when it is in flow. The panoramic view from Sentinel Peak across the Royal Natal National Park is the reason most people make the effort. At seven in the morning, with the mist still breaking below us and the first sunlight catching the tops of the cliffs, it justifies the early start.

article-219.title: Hut to hut across the Tour du Mont Blanc
article-219.introtext: The Tour du Mont Blanc is 164 kilometres of Alpine path connecting France, Italy and Switzerland in a grand loop around the highest mountain in western Europe. I walked it anticlockwise in eleven days in early September, starting from Les Houches with a group of three and finishing there again to the sound of cowbells and the smell of warm fondue from the Chamonix valley below. The route crosses eleven passes above two thousand metres, several of them still holding snow in early September. Each day ends at a refuges or gîte d'étape where dinner is a communal affair and beds are narrow wooden bunks separated by curtains you learn not to trust. The most physically demanding section is the climb from Courmayeur to Grand Col Ferret on day six, a sustained ascent of over a thousand metres on loose scree. The most beautiful is the descent from the Fenêtre d'Arpette into Champex-Lac, a high-alpine traverse that most walkers skip in favour of the standard route via Bovine but which reveals the wildest terrain on the entire circuit.

article-220.title: 48 hours in Porto
article-220.introtext: Two days is just enough to fall for Porto — river light, port lodges and a city that rewards walking.
article-220.fulltext:
Day one: the old town on foot

Start high at the Clerigos tower, then let gravity pull you down the granite lanes toward the Ribeira. The riverfront is all tiled facades and bobbing rabelo boats; cross the Dom Luis I bridge on the upper deck for the view everyone photographs and few earn on foot.

Lunch is a francesinha if you are brave, or grilled sardines and a glass of crisp vinho verde if you are sensible. Spend the afternoon in the port cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia, where a tasting flight of tawny and vintage costs less than a cocktail back home.

Day two: markets, books and the coast

  • Breakfast pastel de nata at a marble-counter cafe near Bolhao market.
  • Livraria Lello early, before the queues, for the staircase that inspired a certain wizarding library.
  • A tram out to Foz do Douro where the river finally meets the Atlantic.

End the trip with an unhurried dinner in Cedofeita, the design district, and a nightcap looking back at the flood-lit bridge. Forty-eight hours in Porto is a tease — most travellers leave already planning the return.

article-221.title: A long weekend in Vienna
article-221.introtext: Imperial grandeur, coffee-house culture and green spaces — Vienna is built for a slow, civilised long weekend.
article-221.fulltext:
The imperial core

Begin inside the Ring, where the Hofburg, the Opera and the museums sit within an easy stroll of one another. Give the Kunsthistorisches an unhurried morning for the Bruegels alone, then recover in a coffee house — a melange and a slice of Sachertorte, newspaper on a wooden holder, no one hurrying you out.

Vienna is a city of rituals, and the coffee house is the one worth adopting. Order slowly and stay long; the waiter in the waistcoat has seen it all before.

Beyond the Ring

  • Schonbrunn gardens at opening time, before the tour buses reach the Gloriette.
  • The Naschmarkt for a lunch of falafel, cheese and pickled everything.
  • A tram ride out to the Prater and one turn on the old Ferris wheel at dusk.

Close the weekend with a standing-room ticket at the Staatsoper — a few euros buys a place under the chandeliers and a story to tell. Vienna does not shout; it simply assumes you will come back, and usually it is right.

article-222.title: A ryokan night in Hakone
article-222.introtext: One night in a Hakone ryokan is less a hotel stay than a small, deliberate ceremony.
article-222.fulltext:
Arrival and the ritual of the evening

You swap your shoes for slippers at the threshold, change into a soft cotton yukata, and the day begins to slow almost against your will. Green tea and a sweet arrive in your tatami room while the mountains do their quiet work through the window.

Dinner is kaiseki — a procession of small, seasonal dishes plated like paintings, each one announced and then left to speak for itself. There is nowhere to be and nothing to check.

The onsen and the morning

  • A soak before dinner, another before bed, and if you can manage it, one more at first light.
  • Rotenburo — the open-air bath — is best in cold weather, steam rising into the pines.
  • Breakfast of grilled fish, rice, miso and pickles, taken kneeling at a low table.

If the weather obliges, Mount Fuji appears in the window like a reward for slowing down. You leave Hakone having done almost nothing, which is exactly the point.

article-223.title: Cliffside rooms in Santorini
article-223.introtext: The cliffside caldera rooms of Santorini earn their fame — and their sunsets — one whitewashed terrace at a time.
article-223.fulltext:
Rooms carved into the cliff

The best places to stay in Oia and Imerovigli are cave houses cut into the volcanic rock, cool in the heat and blindingly white against the blue. A private terrace with a plunge pool is the local currency; the view down the caldera to the sea is the same one that sells a thousand postcards, only this time it is yours before breakfast.

Book the terrace facing west and you have bought a front-row seat to the most over-photographed and still genuinely astonishing sunset in the Aegean.

Beyond the sunset

  • Walk the caldera path from Fira to Oia early, before the cruise crowds land.
  • A boat out to the hot springs and the red-sand beach at Akrotiri.
  • Dinner of grilled octopus and Assyrtiko, the island's mineral white wine.

Santorini is busiest at its edges and quietest just after dawn. Stay two nights, wake early, and you will meet the island the guidebooks promise before everyone else arrives to share it.

article-224.title: A long weekend in the Azores: volcanoes and silence
article-224.introtext: Nine islands adrift in the Atlantic, each one stranger and more beautiful than the last.
article-224.fulltext:
Nine islands, one deep breath

The Azores sit a third of the way to America, green and volcanic and gloriously under-visited. Sao Miguel, the largest, folds around crater lakes — Sete Cidades, twinned blue and green, is the postcard, but the smaller Lagoa do Fogo, reached on foot, is the one you remember.

The weather here does what it likes; locals shrug and call it four seasons in a day. Pack a shell jacket, expect a shower, and be rewarded with rainbows over hydrangea-lined roads.

What to do with a long weekend

  • Soak in the iron-rich thermal pools at Furnas, then eat cozido cooked underground by volcanic steam.
  • Whale-watch off Ponta Delgada — sperm whales and dolphins are near year-round.
  • Hop a short flight to Pico and climb, or simply drink the volcanic wine grown in its lava-walled vineyards.

The Azores reward the unhurried. Give them three days and you will spend the flight home working out when you can give them a week.

article-225.title: Dawn at Angkor: why you must arrive before the crowds
article-225.introtext: The temples at first light belong to nobody — and that is when they reveal everything.
article-225.fulltext:
Why dawn changes everything

By nine the causeway to Angkor Wat is shoulder to shoulder. Arrive in the dark, though, and the great temple belongs to almost no one — a black silhouette that slowly fills with colour as the sky goes from ink to rose behind its five towers, doubled in the reflecting pools.

It is worth the brutal alarm. First light is not just prettier; it is cooler, quieter, and it lets the scale of the place land before the crowds break the spell.

A first-light circuit

  • Angkor Wat for sunrise, then breakfast at a stall while the tour groups arrive.
  • Ta Prohm next, the temple wrapped in strangler-fig roots, before the light goes flat.
  • The Bayon and its serene stone faces mid-morning, then retreat from the heat.

Buy the three-day pass even for a short visit; it lets you go slowly, return to favourites, and skip the midday sun. Angkor is enormous and endlessly detailed — the dawn is simply the door you should walk through first.

article-226.title: Where to eat in Naples: the real pizza city
article-226.introtext: Forget the tourist trail — the best friggitorie and pizzerie are the ones with no signs.
article-226.fulltext:
The city that invented the pizza

Naples does not do pizza as a trend; it does it as a birthright. The classic is disarmingly simple — a marinara with no cheese, or a margherita with San Marzano tomatoes, buffalo mozzarella and a basil leaf, blistered in sixty seconds in a wood oven hotter than seems reasonable. Eat it folded, at a stand-up counter, for a few euros.

The famous names have queues; the neighbourhood pizzerie with no English menu and a nonna at the till are where the city actually eats.

Beyond the pizza

  • Friggitorie for cuoppo — a paper cone of fried seafood and vegetables eaten walking.
  • Sfogliatella, the shell-shaped ricotta pastry, still warm from a Spaccanapoli bakery.
  • A ragu that has simmered since morning, in a trattoria that opens only for lunch.

Follow the smell, ignore the signs, and order what the table next to you is having. Naples rewards appetite and punishes hesitation — arrive hungry and stay that way.

article-227.title: The slow train from Hanoi to Danang
article-227.introtext: Sixteen hours along the coast of Vietnam, with a dining car and no wifi — exactly right.
article-227.fulltext:
Sixteen hours down the coast

The Reunification Express is not fast and does not pretend to be. Between Hanoi and Danang it hugs the coast for the best stretch of railway in Vietnam, sliding past rice terraces, fishing villages and, at the Hai Van Pass, a sudden reveal of sea and mountain that has stopped conversation in the dining car more than once.

There is no wifi to speak of, which is the point. You watch the country go by at the pace it was meant to be seen.

How to ride it well

  • Book a soft-sleeper berth for the overnight leg; four bunks, clean sheets, a shared flask of tea.
  • Bring your own snacks but also try the trolley banh mi and the strong iced coffee.
  • Sit on the seaward side for the Hai Van Pass and set an alarm so you do not sleep through it.

Trains here run late and that is simply how it is. Treat the timetable as a suggestion, and the slow train becomes the part of the trip you talk about most.

article-228.title: Gorilla trekking in Bwindi: closer than you expect
article-228.introtext: An hour in the forest with a mountain gorilla family changes your sense of what is possible.
article-228.fulltext:
An hour that rearranges you

Bwindi Impenetrable Forest is exactly as named — a tangle of ancient rainforest on the Uganda-DRC border, home to nearly half the world's mountain gorillas. Trekking to a habituated family can take one sweaty hour or six, depending on where they have wandered; the guides read broken stems and knuckle-prints like a newspaper.

When you find them, you are given one hour. A silverback the size of a small car regards you with something close to boredom while juveniles tumble through the undergrowth an arm's length away.

Planning the trek

  • Permits are limited and sell out months ahead — book early through a licensed operator.
  • You will need decent boots, gaiters and gloves; the forest earns its name.
  • Hire a porter at the trailhead; it eases the climb and puts money into the community.

It is not a cheap hour, and it is worth every cent. Few wildlife encounters leave you as quietly changed as sharing a hillside with a gorilla family going about its afternoon.

article-229.title: Chasing the northern lights in northern Finland
article-229.introtext: Glass-roofed cabins, reindeer on the lake, and the green curtain shimmering above.
article-229.fulltext:
Waiting for the green curtain

In Finnish Lapland the aurora is a matter of patience and clear skies. From a glass-roofed cabin near Saariselka or Rovaniemi you can lie warm under the duvet and watch the sky, then bolt outside in your thermals when the green begins to shimmer and ripple overhead.

There is no schedule and no guarantee — that is part of the pull. When it comes, the whole sky seems to breathe, and no photograph you take will do it justice.

Making the trip work

  • Go between late September and March, on a multi-night stay to beat the cloud odds.
  • Fill the daylight with huskies, reindeer sleds or a snowmobile across a frozen lake.
  • Download an aurora-forecast app and dress in real layers — minus twenty is normal.

Even on a quiet night, Lapland delivers: reindeer on the ice, silence you can hear, and a sky so full of stars the aurora almost seems like showing off. Give it three or four nights and the odds tip firmly in your favour.

article-230.title: Marrakech beyond the medina: riads, gardens and quiet corners
article-230.introtext: The souks are spectacular. The palmerie at dusk is where you will want to stay forever.
article-230.fulltext:
Past the souks

The medina's souks are a glorious assault — spice pyramids, hammered lanterns, the call to prayer over it all — but Marrakech reveals its softer self the moment you step off the main drag. Duck through an unmarked door and a riad opens into a cool, tiled courtyard with an orange tree and a fountain, the noise of the city suddenly a rumour.

Stay in one and the rhythm of the city changes: mint tea on the roof at dusk, breakfast of msemen and honey in the shade, the crowds only a choice away.

Quiet corners to find

  • The Jardin Majorelle and the smaller, calmer Le Jardin Secret in the medina.
  • A hammam scrub-and-steam, the local reset that no spa abroad matches.
  • The Palmeraie at dusk, palm groves gold in the last light beyond the walls.

Bargain hard but kindly, get pleasantly lost, and always accept the tea. Marrakech is loud where it wants to be and serene where you least expect it — the trick is knowing when to step through the door.

article-231.title: Japan's Kumano Kodo pilgrim trails
article-231.introtext: Japan's Kumano Kodo is not one trail but a web of ancient pilgrimage routes threading the forested Kii Peninsula — walked for over a thousand years by emperors and commoners alike toward the three grand shrines of Kumano.
article-231.fulltext:
Most walkers start on the Nakahechi route from Takijiri-oji, where a small shrine marks the point pilgrims once believed they crossed into the sacred mountains. The path climbs immediately into cedar and cypress, the light going green and the city falling away within minutes.

Walking between the oji

The route is punctuated by oji — subsidiary shrines where pilgrims once stopped to pray and rest. Today they make natural waypoints, each with a weathered marker and often a bench worn smooth by centuries of tired legs. Between them the forest does the work of quieting your mind.

You sleep in family-run minshuku in mountain villages, where dinner is a dozen small dishes of river fish, mountain vegetables and rice, and the bath is scalding and communal. It is a walk measured in hospitality as much as kilometres.

The pilgrimage is less about arriving than about the rhythm of walking itself — one foot, then the other, under trees older than the shrines.

What the days actually look like

A typical Nakahechi itinerary runs four to five days at a gentle pace. The walking is rarely technical but the climbs are long, and the humidity in summer is real. Come in late autumn for cool air and maple colour, or spring for the cherry and the fresh green.

  • Day 1 — Takijiri-oji to Takahara, the "village in the mist", for sunset over the ridges.
  • Day 2 — Takahara to Chikatsuyu, the longest forest section.
  • Day 3 — over the Mikoshi-toge pass down to Hongu and the vast Oyunohara torii gate.
  • Day 4 — a river boat or the Kohechi high route toward Nachi and its waterfall shrine.

Practicalities

Buses link the trailheads to Kii-Tanabe station, which connects to Osaka in about two hours. Book minshuku well ahead in peak seasons — the villages are tiny and beds are few. Carry cash, a light rain shell, and a dual-pilgrim credential if you also plan to walk the Camino de Santiago, with which Kumano is formally twinned.

article-232.title: Crossing Corsica end to end on the GR20
article-232.introtext: Rated among Europe's most demanding long-distance trails, the GR20 traces a rocky spine from Calenzana in the north to Conca in the south across fifteen days of sustained mountain terrain. I walked the full route in late September when the summer crowds had thinned but the high refuges were still open. The northern section tests your nerve: exposed granite ridges, chain-assisted descents, and the psychological toll of sustained altitude. The southern half opens into broader valleys and longer meadow sections, rewarding those who have earned their legs on the first week. Water sources can be scarce on certain northern stages; carry at least two litres between marked streams. Budget for hut accommodation as wild camping is restricted in the national park. The finish in Conca feels earned in a way that few trails anywhere can match.

article-233.title: Island-hopping the Cyclades by ferry
article-233.introtext: The trick to the Cyclades isn't choosing one island — it's stringing together three or four with the slow blue-hulled ferries that have linked these whitewashed ports for generations.
article-233.fulltext:
Start in Naxos for the long sand beaches and the marble villages of the interior, then take the morning boat to tiny Koufonisia where the water turns an impossible turquoise over a flat sandy seabed.

From there, Amorgos rewards anyone who climbs to the Hozoviotissa monastery clinging to a vertical cliff. End in Santorini if you must, but the real magic is in the quiet stops most cruise crowds skip.

Book deck-class tickets a day ahead in peak summer, carry cash for the smaller harbours, and never plan a tight connection — the Aegean meltemi wind reshuffles schedules without apology.

article-234.title: Tracking black rhino on foot in Damaraland
article-234.introtext: There is no vehicle, no fence and no guarantee. Tracking desert-adapted black rhino on foot across Namibia's Damaraland is the most humbling wildlife encounter we know.
article-234.fulltext:
You set out at first light with a community tracker who reads three-day-old prints in the gravel like a newspaper. The landscape is vast and ochre, broken only by welwitschia plants older than most cities.

When you finally crest a rise and see a rhino browsing two hundred metres downwind, the silence is total. You watch, you photograph, you back away — the animal never knows you were there.

The trackers are employed by the same conservancies that protect these rhino from poaching, so every booking funds the patrols. It is conservation you can feel under your boots.

Good to know

  • Trek on foot with a community tracker; distance and success vary with the wind and the rhino.
  • Go in the cooler dawn hours and carry water, sun cover and boots that grip the gravel.
  • Book through a conservancy so your fee funds the anti-poaching patrols.

article-235.title: The Bergen Line: Oslo to the fjords by rail
article-235.introtext: Seven hours, four hundred kilometres and one of the great train journeys of Europe — the Bergen Line climbs from the Oslo woodlands onto a snow-blasted plateau and down to the rain-bright western coast.
article-235.fulltext:
The highlight is Finse, the highest station on the line at 1,222 metres, where the Hardangerjokulen glacier glints beyond the platform and even summer mornings carry a bite.

Most travellers break the trip at Myrdal to ride the Flam Railway, a steep branch line that corkscrews down to a fjord arm past the thundering Kjosfossen waterfall.

Reserve a window seat on the right heading west, bring a thermos, and don't bury yourself in a book — the scenery changes every fifteen minutes.

Good to know

  • Reserve seats ahead; the Oslo-Bergen service and the Flam branch both fill in summer.
  • Break the journey at Myrdal for the Flam Railway and a night by the fjord.
  • Even in summer, pack a warm layer for the Finse plateau.

article-236.title: A day eating through Oaxaca's markets
article-236.introtext: Oaxaca rewards the hungry. Spend a day moving between its markets and you'll taste mole in seven shades, tlayudas the size of bicycle wheels and mezcal poured straight from the still.
article-236.fulltext:
Begin at Mercado 20 de Noviembre, where the smoke-filled 'pasillo de humo' lets you choose raw cuts of meat and have them grilled in front of you, eaten with charred spring onions and warm tortillas.

Mid-morning, hunt down a cup of frothy cacao with a sweet bread at a side stall. By afternoon you should be at a mezcaleria learning to tell an espadin from a tobala by smell alone.

Go gently. The food here is generous and the mezcal is honest — pace both, and leave room for an evening tamale from a doorway comal.

Good to know

  • Start early at Mercado 20 de Noviembre before the pasillo de humo fills with smoke.
  • Pace the mezcal; tastings are generous and the spirit is stronger than it seems.
  • Carry small pesos for the stalls and leave room for an evening tamale.

article-237.title: Mexico City in 72 hours: design, tacos and Frida
article-237.introtext: Few cities pack so much into a long weekend. Mexico City layers Aztec ruins, Art Deco neighbourhoods and a food scene that runs from street-corner suadero to tasting menus that top global lists.
article-237.fulltext:
Base yourself in Roma or Condesa, leafy grids of jacaranda trees, independent bookshops and the kind of cafes you'll be reluctant to leave. Walk everywhere — this is a city best read at street level.

Give a full morning to the Frida Kahlo Museum in Coyoacan (book online, it sells out), and a sunset to the rooftops around the Centro Historico where the cathedral floats above the lights.

Eat tacos al pastor where the trompo is busiest, and never skip a tlacoyo from a comal aunty even if you've just eaten.

Good to know

  • Base in Roma or Condesa and walk; the metro covers the longer hops cheaply.
  • Book the Frida Kahlo Museum online days ahead, as it sells out.
  • Eat tacos al pastor where the trompo is busiest and the queue is local.

article-238.title: Trekking the Laugavegur trail across Iceland's highlands
article-238.introtext: Iceland's most famous multi-day hike runs 55 kilometres through a landscape that looks freshly made — rhyolite mountains streaked yellow and red, black sand deserts and glacial rivers you ford barefoot.
article-238.fulltext:
The classic route runs north to south from Landmannalaugar to Thorsmork over four days, with mountain huts spaced a comfortable walk apart. Book hut beds months ahead; the alternative is a tent and Icelandic weather.

Day two crosses the otherworldly obsidian fields below Hrafntinnusker, often under snow even in July. The reward is the descent into the green valley of Alftavatn, a lake the colour of pewter.

Pack for four seasons in one day, carry quick-dry layers for the river crossings, and watch the wind forecast — it, not the rain, decides whether you walk.

Good to know

  • Book hut beds months ahead, or carry a tent rated for real wind.
  • Pack quick-dry layers and sandals for the barefoot river fords.
  • Check the wind forecast daily; it, not the rain, decides the day.

article-239.title: Sleeping in a converted lighthouse on the Brittany coast
article-239.introtext: Some stays are about the room; this one is about the weather. A converted signal house on Brittany's wild Finistere coast trades minibars and room service for storm-watching and the smell of salt.
article-239.fulltext:
The keeper's quarters have been reworked with linen, slate and a wood stove, but the bones are unchanged — thick granite walls, deep window seats and a spiral stair to the old lamp room.

Mornings begin with oysters from the bay below and end with a fire as the lighthouse beam still sweeps overhead. There is no television and the wifi is poetic.

Come in the shoulder seasons for the drama. A spring gale against that glass, mug of cider in hand, is worth more than any five-star spa.

Good to know

  • Come in the shoulder seasons for the storms and the empty coast path.
  • Bring layers and a book; there is no television and little signal.
  • Time low tide for the oyster beds and rock pools below the house.

article-240.title: How to plan a first safari without overspending
article-240.introtext: A safari has a reputation for being out of reach. With a little planning it needn't be — the difference between a dream trip and a budget-buster usually comes down to timing, location and how you sleep.
article-240.fulltext:
Travel in the green season (roughly November to March in East Africa) when lodges cut rates by half and the landscape is lush and full of newborn animals. The game viewing is excellent if you accept occasional rain.

Choose one well-stocked park and stay put rather than racing between three. Fewer transfers means lower cost and more time actually watching wildlife.

Public or 'budget' tented camps inside the parks cost a fraction of the luxury lodges and put you closer to the dawn chorus. Spend the saving on a great guide — that, more than thread count, makes the trip.

article-241.title: Slow days on the Andaman beaches of Koh Lanta
article-241.introtext: Koh Lanta is the antidote to Thailand's party islands — a long, lazy strip of west-facing beaches where the day's biggest decision is which sunset bar to claim.
article-241.fulltext:
The southern beaches are quietest, fringed by national park forest and reached by a coast road that gets gloriously rough toward the end. Rent a scooter and let the day unspool.

Old Town on the east coast is the cultural heart, a row of stilted Chinese-Thai shophouses over the water serving fish so fresh it was swimming at lunch.

Come outside the November-to-April high season and you'll have whole bays to yourself, though some beach bars shutter for the monsoon.

Good to know

  • Rent a scooter for the rough southern coast road and the national-park beaches.
  • Visit outside the November-to-April high season for near-empty bays.
  • Cross to Old Town for stilted seafood served over the water.

article-242.title: Snorkelling with whale sharks off Mafia Island
article-242.introtext: Tanzania's Mafia Island keeps a remarkable secret: a resident population of whale sharks that feed near the surface for much of the year, close enough to a small boat that you simply slip in beside them.
article-242.fulltext:
These are the largest fish in the ocean, gentle filter feeders the length of a bus, and swimming alongside one as it cruises through clouds of plankton recalibrates your sense of scale.

The best months are October to March when the sharks aggregate in the channel. Responsible operators cap swimmer numbers and keep a respectful distance — choose them.

Mafia is also a serious diving destination, with a marine park protecting some of the healthiest coral in the Indian Ocean. Stay a few extra days; getting here is half the effort.

Good to know

  • The best months are October to March, when the sharks gather in the channel.
  • Choose operators who cap swimmer numbers and keep a respectful distance.
  • Stay extra days for the marine-park diving; getting here is half the effort.

article-243.title: Riding the Death Railway through Kanchanaburi
article-243.introtext: Few train lines carry as much weight as the one that crosses the River Kwai. The surviving stretch of Thailand's wartime railway is now a sombre, beautiful day journey through jungle and along a clifftop trestle.
article-243.fulltext:
The most dramatic section is the Wampo viaduct, a wooden shelf bolted to a sheer limestone face above the river, where the carriages lean out over the water.

Pair the ride with the thoughtful Thailand-Burma Railway Centre in Kanchanaburi and the immaculately kept war cemetery; the line's history of forced labour deserves more than a photo stop.

Sit on the right heading toward Nam Tok for the river views, and travel early before the heat builds in the open carriages.

Good to know

  • Sit on the right toward Nam Tok for the Wampo viaduct and river views.
  • Travel early, before the open carriages heat up.
  • Pair the ride with the railway centre and war cemetery in Kanchanaburi.

article-244.title: Eating your way around a Lisbon tasca crawl
article-244.introtext: Forget the tourist-menu boards near the castle. Real Lisbon eating happens in the tascas — tiny family tabernas where the day's catch is chalked on a board and the house wine arrives without asking.
article-244.fulltext:
Start in Alfama with a plate of grilled sardines and broa bread, then climb to a tasca in Graca for bacalhau a bras, salt cod tangled with eggs and matchstick potatoes.

Finish in a Bairro Alto cervejaria over a bowl of garlicky clams and a cold imperial beer, the city tumbling downhill outside the door.

Lunch is the locals' big meal, so go midday for the prato do dia, and never leave a tasca without an espresso and a pastel de nata.

Good to know

  • Go at midday for the locals' prato do dia, the day's best value.
  • Order the house wine and whatever is chalked on the board.
  • Never leave a tasca without an espresso and a pastel de nata.

article-245.title: A long weekend in Seville: orange trees and flamenco
article-245.introtext: Seville is built for a long weekend — compact enough to walk, theatrical enough to fill three days, and warm enough that life happens outdoors well into the night.
article-245.fulltext:
Lose a morning in the Real Alcazar's tiled courtyards and the cathedral's orange-tree patio, then escape the midday heat the local way, with a long lunch and a slow vermouth.

Evenings belong to the tapas crawl through Triana and the back streets of Santa Cruz, and to an intimate flamenco tablao where the floorboards do half the singing.

Go in spring or autumn; high summer turns the city into a furnace by noon and even the locals retreat indoors.

Good to know

  • Visit in spring or autumn; high summer bakes the city by noon.
  • Book the Real Alcazar online to skip the long queue.
  • Save flamenco for an intimate tablao rather than the big tourist shows.

article-246.title: Walking the Nakasendo between Magome and Tsumago
article-246.introtext: The Nakasendo once linked Kyoto and Edo across the mountains, and the cobbled stretch between the post towns of Magome and Tsumago is the most rewarding day walk on the whole route.
article-246.fulltext:
It's an easy eight kilometres through cedar forest and rice terraces, past waterfalls and a working bear bell you ring to announce yourself. The grade is gentle and the way-marking faultless.

Both towns have been beautifully preserved as Edo-period streetscapes, all dark timber inns and stone gutters running with mountain water. Stay overnight in a minshuku for the full effect.

A handy service forwards your main bag between the towns so you walk light, and the local buses fill any gaps if the weather turns.

Good to know

  • Walk Magome to Tsumago downhill; it is an easy eight kilometres.
  • Use the bag-forwarding service between the towns and walk light.
  • Stay a night in a minshuku for the full Edo-era effect.

article-247.title: Inside a restored riad in the Marrakech medina
article-247.introtext: Step off a noisy derb and through an unmarked door, and the medina falls silent. A restored riad turns its back on the street and inward to a cool courtyard of citrus trees, tilework and trickling water.
article-247.fulltext:
The best riads are family-run and small — half a dozen rooms around the central court, a rooftop for breakfast under the Atlas light and a hammam in the basement for the dust of the souks.

Yours might once have been a single merchant's home, the rooms now individually styled with tadelakt plaster, carved cedar and lanterns that throw lace patterns at night.

Book one with a daytime concierge who can arrange a guide for the first foray into the souks — finding your way back is the real Marrakech rite of passage.

Good to know

  • Choose a small, family-run riad with a rooftop terrace and a hammam.
  • Arrange a daytime guide for your first foray into the souks.
  • Expect to get lost finding your way back; that is the rite of passage.

article-248.title: What to pack for a cold-weather trek (and what to leave)
article-248.introtext: The mistake most first-time cold-weather trekkers make isn't packing too little — it's packing too much of the wrong thing. Warmth on the trail is about layering, not bulk.
article-248.fulltext:
Build from a thin merino base, a fleece or light down mid-layer and a genuinely waterproof shell. Three smart layers beat one heavy coat because you can dump heat fast on the climbs.

Your extremities decide your comfort: spare dry socks, liner gloves under shells, and a warm hat weigh almost nothing and change everything. Skip the cotton entirely; once wet it stays wet.

Leave the spare boots, the third book and the just-in-case gadgets. Every kilo on your back is a kilo you carry uphill — ruthless packing is a kindness to your future self.

Good to know

  • Build three layers: a merino base, light insulation and a waterproof shell.
  • Prioritise spare dry socks, liner gloves and a warm hat.
  • Leave the cotton, the spare boots and the just-in-case gadgets at home.

article-249.title: Finding the quiet beaches of the Algarve
article-249.introtext: The Algarve's postcard coves get all the attention, but step west of the resorts and Portugal's south coast turns wild — empty surf beaches backed by cliffs and a single shack selling grilled fish.
article-249.fulltext:
The Costa Vicentina, a protected stretch running up the Atlantic-facing west, is where locals go. The water is colder and the swell bigger, but the beaches are vast and often deserted.

Base yourself in a low-key town like Sagres or Aljezur, walk a section of the Rota Vicentina clifftop trail, and time your beach days around the tide for the biggest swathes of sand.

Go in June or September for warm water and thin crowds; August belongs to the families and the car parks fill by ten.

Good to know

  • Head to the Costa Vicentina, west of the resorts, for empty Atlantic sand.
  • Base in Sagres or Aljezur and walk a stretch of the Rota Vicentina.
  • Come in June or September for warm water and thin crowds.

article-250.title: Birding the cloud forest of Monteverde
article-250.introtext: Costa Rica's Monteverde is a forest with its head in the clouds — a dripping green world of mosses and bromeliads where the resplendent quetzal, the most coveted bird in the Americas, still nests.
article-250.fulltext:
Walk the reserve trails at dawn with a guide who knows the quetzal's favourite wild avocado trees, and you stand a real chance of seeing that impossible green-and-crimson tail in flight.

Beyond the headline bird, the forest hums with hummingbirds, bellbirds and the occasional troop of capuchins. The famous hanging bridges put you up in the canopy where much of the action happens.

Bring a rain shell whatever the forecast — 'cloud forest' is a literal description — and binoculars you trust. The light is dim and the birds are quick.

Good to know

  • Walk the reserve at dawn with a guide who knows the quetzal's avocado trees.
  • Bring a proper rain shell; the cloud forest lives up to its name.
  • Pack binoculars you trust, as the light is dim and the birds are quick.

article-251.title: The Tazara Railway: Dar es Salaam to the Zambian border
article-251.introtext: Few journeys cut across Africa like the Tazara, a Cold War-era line that rattles from the Indian Ocean coast through the Selous game reserve and up onto the Zambian plateau over two unhurried days.
article-251.fulltext:
The great surprise is the wildlife: the train slices through the southern reaches of a vast reserve, and from the dining car you may spot elephant, giraffe and impala between courses.

Travel in a first-class four-berth cabin, befriend the dining-car staff, and accept that the timetable is a suggestion. The point is the slow unspooling of the continent outside the window.

Stock up on snacks and water in Dar, carry small notes for the platform vendors who appear at every halt, and let the rhythm of the rails reset your pace.

Good to know

  • Book a first-class four-berth cabin and settle in for two unhurried days.
  • Watch for elephant and giraffe where the line crosses the reserve.
  • Stock snacks and small notes in Dar for the platform vendors.

article-252.title: Forty-eight hours in Edinburgh's old and new towns
article-252.introtext: Edinburgh splits neatly in two — the brooding medieval Old Town piling up toward the castle, and the elegant Georgian New Town laid out in honey-stone crescents. Two days lets you do justice to both.
article-252.fulltext:
Spend the first morning climbing the Royal Mile to the castle, then duck into the closes and underground vaults that thread beneath it. Afternoon belongs to Arthur's Seat for the city laid out below.

Cross to the New Town for the second day: independent shops on Thistle Street, the Scottish National Gallery, and a dram tasting that explains why this city takes its whisky seriously.

Pack for all four seasons regardless of month, book a table for dinner, and end on Calton Hill at sunset when the whole skyline turns gold.

Good to know

  • Pack for four seasons whatever the month says.
  • Climb Arthur's Seat early and save Calton Hill for sunset.
  • Book dinner ahead, especially during the festival season.

article-253.title: The hill villages of Tuscany on two wheels
article-253.introtext: Cypress-lined gravel roads link the medieval hill towns of central Tuscany, and a bicycle is the perfect pace to ride between them.
article-253.fulltext:
The pace of a bicycle

Cypress-lined gravel roads link the medieval hill towns of central Tuscany, and a bicycle is the perfect pace to ride between them — fast enough to cover ground, slow enough to smell the wild fennel and stop for the view of the next town stacked on its ridge.

Set off early from Siena before the heat, climbing gently through vineyards and olive groves toward the famous towers of San Gimignano on the horizon.

A day in the saddle

  • Mid-morning espresso in a piazza where the barista knows every passing cyclist.
  • A long lunch of pici pasta and a glass of the local Chianti, then a shady rest.
  • The gravel Strade Bianche between Asciano and Montalcino for the classic ride.

The afternoon is mostly downhill home, legs tired and camera full. You do not need to be fast here — a gravel bike, a rough map and a willingness to climb are enough to make Tuscany feel, for a few days, entirely your own.

article-254.title: Temple-hopping by bicycle in Bagan
article-254.introtext: More than two thousand temples spread across the Bagan plain, and an e-bike lets you find your own quiet pagoda for sunrise.
article-254.fulltext:
Two thousand temples, one flat plain

Bagan spreads more than two thousand brick temples and stupas across a dusty plain beside the Irrawaddy, and the best way to reach the quiet ones is by bicycle — or an e-bike if the heat has beaten you. Away from the famous few, you can prop the bike against a thousand-year-old shrine and have it entirely to yourself.

The light does the heavy lifting: at dawn the plain fills with mist and the temples float; at dusk everything turns the colour of the bricks.

Riding the plain

  • Start at first light while it is cool and the crowds are still at the big viewpoints.
  • Carry more water than you think you need — shade is scarce between temples.
  • Follow the sandy side tracks; the emptiest temples are rarely the signposted ones.

Bagan rewards wandering over ticking off a list. Pick a direction, ride until a temple pulls you in, climb where you are allowed, and let the plain unfold at bicycle speed.

article-255.title: Driving the Carretera Austral through Patagonia
article-255.introtext: Chile's wild southern highway threads through rainforest, glaciers and turquoise rivers, mostly on gravel and entirely on its own terms.
article-255.fulltext:
The road at the end of the world

Chile's Carretera Austral runs for some 1,200 kilometres through northern Patagonia, much of it gravel, all of it spectacular — a ribbon of road threading temperate rainforest, hanging glaciers and rivers the colour of mouthwash. It is a drive to be savoured, not rushed; the surface alone keeps you honest.

Between towns there is often nothing but forest and the occasional gaucho on horseback, which is precisely why people come.

Driving it well

  • Hire a high-clearance vehicle and carry a spare tyre, fuel and food — services are thin.
  • Detour to the Marble Caves on Lake General Carrera, best by boat in the morning calm.
  • Build in slack days for weather and washouts; the road does not always cooperate.

Allow at least a week and resist the urge to cover distance. The Carretera Austral is one of the great road trips precisely because the driving is slow, the traffic is almost none, and every bend seems to offer a reason to stop.
article-255.metadesc: Chile's wild southern highway threads through rainforest, glaciers and turquoise rivers, mostly on gravel and entirely on its own terms.

article-256.title: Felucca nights on the Nile near Aswan
article-256.introtext: A felucca, the lateen-sailed boat of the Nile, offers the slowest and finest way to drift past Aswan's islands and temples.
article-256.fulltext:
Sailing the Nile the old way

A felucca is the traditional wooden sailboat of the Nile, and a night aboard one near Aswan is the antidote to the cruise-ship version of Egypt. There is no engine and no schedule — the boatman reads the wind, you lie back on cushions, and the river slides by past palm-fringed islands and villages where children wave from the bank.

As the sun drops, the sails glow and the temperature finally eases. Dinner is simple, cooked on board, eaten by lamplight.

A night on the water

  • Sail up to Elephantine Island and the Nubian villages with their painted houses.
  • Bring a warm layer — desert nights are cold even when the days are furnace-hot.
  • Sleep on deck under a mosquito net and wake to mist rising off the river.

It is rustic, unhurried and gloriously low-tech. For a night or two, the felucca strips Egypt back to wind, water and a horizon of date palms — the way travellers have crossed this stretch of the Nile for centuries.

article-257.title: A street-food morning in Penang's George Town
article-257.introtext: George Town's hawker stalls are a UNESCO-worthy collision of Malay, Chinese and Indian cooking, best tackled on an empty stomach at breakfast.
article-257.fulltext:
Breakfast on the hoof

George Town wakes up hungry. By seven the hawker stalls of Penang's old quarter are firing up woks and charcoal grills, and the smart move is to eat your way from one to the next — a small plate here, a bowl there, following the queues of locals who know exactly which uncle makes the best char kway teow.

This is a food culture built on centuries of Malay, Chinese, Indian and Peranakan mingling, and it shows up on every plate.

What to order

  • Char kway teow — smoky flat noodles with prawns and cockles, wok-hei and all.
  • Asam laksa, sour and fishy and unforgettable, from a stall by the market.
  • Roti canai with dhal, and a frothy teh tarik pulled high between two cups.

Eat little and often, drink the pulled tea, and do not fill up at the first stall. A George Town food morning is a crawl, not a meal — pace yourself and the city rewards you with one of the great street-food breakfasts in Asia.
article-257.metadesc: George Town's hawker stalls are a UNESCO-worthy collision of Malay, Chinese and Indian cooking, best tackled on an empty stomach at breakfast.

article-258.title: Via ferrata in the Italian Dolomites
article-258.introtext: The Dolomites' network of cabled climbing routes lets walkers reach airy summits once reserved for mountaineers.
article-258.fulltext:
Iron rungs and airy ledges

The via ferrata — literally the iron way — lets walkers with a head for heights travel routes that would otherwise need a rope and real climbing skill. The Dolomites are its birthplace, laced with steel cables, ladders and pegs first strung across the peaks during the First World War, now a playground of vertical rock and impossible views.

Clipped to the cable with a harness and lanyard, you move along ledges and up chimneys with the valley falling away beneath your boots.

Before you clip in

  • Hire a guide for your first routes and rent a proper via ferrata set — harness, lanyard, helmet.
  • Start with an easier graded route to learn the clipping rhythm before the exposed classics.
  • Watch the afternoon storms; be off the high routes before the weather turns.

You do not need to be a climber, but you do need steady nerves and basic fitness. Get both right and the Dolomites open up a way of moving through the mountains that feels equal parts hiking and flying.

article-259.title: Watching mountain gorillas in Volcanoes National Park
article-259.introtext: An hour with a habituated gorilla family on the slopes of Rwanda's volcanoes is among the most moving wildlife encounters on earth.
article-259.fulltext:
Face to face in the Virungas

Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park protects a slice of the Virunga range and the mountain gorillas made famous by Dian Fossey. The trek starts among terraced potato fields and climbs into thick bamboo and Hagenia forest, where the guides track a habituated family by the trail of bent stems and fresh feeding signs.

The reward is an hour in their company — a silverback dozing in a clearing, mothers cradling infants, blackbacks thumping past close enough to feel the ground shift.

Making it happen

  • Permits are premium-priced and capped daily; book well ahead through the park or an operator.
  • The trek can be short or a steep half-day — a reasonable level of fitness helps.
  • Base yourself in Musanze the night before for the early morning briefing.

Rwanda has poured gorilla-tourism revenue back into conservation and community, and it shows in the mountain. An hour with the Virunga gorillas is expensive, humbling and, by every account, unforgettable.
article-259.metadesc: An hour with a habituated gorilla family on the slopes of Rwanda's volcanoes is among the most moving wildlife encounters on earth.

article-260.title: A perfect day in Porto without the queues
article-260.introtext: Porto packs azulejo-tiled churches, port lodges and river views into a city you can cover on foot in a single, well-planned day.
article-260.fulltext:
Porto without the queues

Porto packs azulejo-tiled churches, port lodges and river views into a city you can cover on foot in a single, well-planned day — if you time it to dodge the crowds. Start high and early at the Clerigos tower, then wind down through the Ribeira to the river before the tour groups fill the lanes.

The trick is to front-load the famous sights and save the eating and drinking for when everyone else is queueing.

A day that flows

  • Cross the iron Dom Luis I bridge on the upper deck for the classic caldera-of-the-city view.
  • A tasting at a Gaia port cellar in the late morning, before the afternoon rush.
  • Grilled sardines and vinho verde by the water as the light goes gold.

End with a slow walk back over the bridge as the lodges light up across the Douro. Porto is small enough to do in a day and generous enough to make you wish you had booked a second — plan it well and you get the best of both.
article-260.metadesc: Porto packs azulejo-tiled churches, port lodges and river views into a city you can cover on foot in a single, well-planned day.

article-261.title: Crossing Switzerland on the Glacier Express
article-261.introtext: Billed as the slowest express train in the world, the Glacier Express takes eight unhurried hours to cross the Alps from Zermatt to St Moritz.
article-261.fulltext:
The slowest express in the world

The Glacier Express earns its cheerful nickname by taking nearly eight hours to travel between Zermatt and St Moritz — a journey you could drive far faster and would never want to. Instead you sit under panoramic glass as the train climbs through 91 tunnels and over 291 bridges, including the graceful Landwasser viaduct that curves straight into a cliff face.

Switzerland unrolls at window height: deep gorges, alpine meadows, and the Oberalp Pass at over two thousand metres.

Riding in comfort

  • Reserve a window seat well ahead; the panoramic carriages sell out in summer.
  • Take the optional lunch served at your seat as the scenery slides past.
  • Sit on the right leaving Zermatt for the best of the early valley views.

It is not cheap and it is not fast, and that is entirely the appeal. The Glacier Express turns crossing the Alps into the destination itself — a day-long, unhurried glide through the postcard heart of Switzerland.
article-261.metadesc: Billed as the slowest express train in the world, the Glacier Express takes eight unhurried hours to cross the Alps from Zermatt to St Moritz.

article-262.title: Travelling Vietnam end to end on a budget
article-262.introtext: Vietnam rewards the thrifty traveller: cheap sleeper trains, dollar bowls of pho and guesthouses that cost less than a city coffee back home.
article-262.fulltext:
The whole country on a shoestring

Vietnam is one of the great value destinations, and travelling it end to end — Hanoi in the north to the Mekong Delta in the south — can be done comfortably on a modest budget. Overnight trains and sleeper buses cover the long distances cheaply and save you a night's accommodation into the bargain.

Street food is the secret: a bowl of pho or a banh mi costs a couple of dollars and beats most restaurant meals hands down.

Stretching the budget

  • Take the Reunification Express in stages; soft-sleeper berths are cheap and comfortable.
  • Eat where the plastic stools are full of locals, not where the menu has photos.
  • Rent a motorbike for a day in places like Ha Giang or the Hai Van Pass.

Allow three or four weeks to do it justice without rushing. Travel slowly, eat on the street, take the night transport, and Vietnam gives you an extraordinary amount of country for very little money.
article-262.metadesc: Vietnam rewards the thrifty traveller: cheap sleeper trains, dollar bowls of pho and guesthouses that cost less than a city coffee back home.

article-263.title: A night in a tented lodge on the Maasai Mara
article-263.introtext: A classic safari lodge trades walls for canvas, putting you within earshot of the Mara's lions while you sleep under crisp linen.
article-263.fulltext:
Under canvas on the Mara

A tented lodge on the Maasai Mara is safari at its most romantic — proper beds and hot showers, but only a sweep of canvas between you and the sounds of the plain at night. Lions call in the dark, hippos grunt from the river, and you drift off feeling gloriously exposed to a wilderness that is very much awake.

By day the Mara delivers the classic East African spectacle: lion prides, elephant herds and, in season, the great wildebeest migration churning across the grass.

Days on the plain

  • Dawn game drives when the predators are still active and the light is soft.
  • A bush breakfast laid out on the savanna between morning sightings.
  • Sundowners on a rise as the sky goes orange and the day's animals settle.

Choose a camp in a conservancy bordering the reserve for fewer vehicles and walking safaris. A few nights under canvas on the Mara is the safari most people picture before they ever go — and it lives up to it.
article-263.metadesc: A classic safari lodge trades walls for canvas, putting you within earshot of the Mara's lions while you sleep under crisp linen.

article-264.title: A ryokan night and a private onsen in Hakone
article-264.introtext: A Hakone ryokan distils Japanese hospitality into one evening: a tatami room, a multi-course kaiseki dinner and a steaming private onsen with a mountain view.
article-264.fulltext:
An evening built around a bath

A Hakone ryokan distils Japanese hospitality into a single evening: a tatami room, a multi-course kaiseki dinner and a steaming private onsen with a mountain view. You change into a yukata on arrival, soak before dinner and again before bed, and let the ritual slow you right down.

The private onsen is the luxury worth paying for — your own open-air bath, booked for an hour, steam rising into the cold night while the rest of the inn sleeps.

The rhythm of a stay

  • Green tea and a sweet on arrival, then a long soak before the evening meal.
  • Kaiseki dinner served in your room or a private dining space, course by course.
  • A final dawn bath, then breakfast of grilled fish, rice and pickles.

Wake to Mount Fuji framed in the window if the weather obliges. One night is enough to reset you completely — the ryokan asks nothing of you but that you slow down and pay attention, which turns out to be the whole holiday.
article-264.metadesc: A Hakone ryokan distils Japanese hospitality into one evening: a tatami room, a multi-course kaiseki dinner and a steaming private onsen with a mountain vi

article-268.fulltext:

article-273.title: The West Highland Way: A Hundred Miles Into the Scottish Highlands
article-273.introtext: Ninety-six miles from the outskirts of Glasgow to the foot of Ben Nevis, Scotland's oldest long-distance path earns its reputation one boggy mile at a time.
article-273.fulltext:
I started at Milngavie, the unglamorous suburban trailhead marked by a granite obelisk, and within two days the path had already traded pavement for the open moor of Rannoch. The route runs north along Loch Lomond's eastern shore, a section locals warn you about more than any other, since it narrows to a scramble over tree roots and boulders for several hours near Inversnaid.

Camping wild is legal and common here, and I pitched most nights within sight of water: Loch Lomond, Loch Tulla, the River Orchy. The middle days across Rannoch Moor are the emotional heart of the walk, a flat expanse of heather and old drove roads with Buachaille Etive Mòr rising like a broken tooth on the horizon.

Book the Kingshouse or Inveroran for at least one night if you'd rather have a bed and a dram than a tent — both sit right on the route and fill up fast in summer. The path ends in Fort William beneath Ben Nevis, and if your legs have anything left, the extra day up Britain's highest mountain is worth tacking on before the bus home.

article-274.title: Crossing Norway's Besseggen Ridge in Jotunheimen
article-274.introtext: The knife-edge above two impossibly blue lakes is Norway's most photographed day hike, and it earns every one of its warnings.
article-274.fulltext:
I based myself at the Gjendesheim lodge on the shore of Lake Gjende and caught the first boat across to Memurubu, which is how almost everyone tackles Besseggen — the ridge is far harder walked the other direction. From Memurubu the trail climbs fast through scree to the saddle below Besshø, and for a long, exposed stretch you're balanced on a ridge with Lake Bessvatnet dropping turquoise on one side and Gjende a darker blue nearly four hundred metres below on the other.

The scramble sections aren't technical, but they're airy enough that I stopped noticing the cold and started noticing my hands on the rock instead. Cloud rolls in off the Jotunheimen peaks with little warning, and I met a Norwegian guide who turns back parties the moment visibility drops below the next cairn.

Do it as a long day from Gjendesheim rather than trying to add huts — the DNT cabins nearby are better used before or after for the wider Jotunheimen network, with Glitterheim and Memurubu both good bookends. Go in August; the snow patches that linger into July make the ridge crossing considerably more serious.

article-275.title: The Walker's Haute Route: Chamonix to Zermatt on Foot
article-275.introtext: Between Chamonix and Zermatt lie two weeks, six high passes, and views of the Mont Blanc massif and the Matterhorn from opposite ends of the same walk.
article-275.fulltext:
I split the route into eleven stages and stayed in a mix of refuges and small village hotels, the usual compromise between the ski-touring version's mountain huts and a gentler summer itinerary. The high point is the Col de Riedmatten above Arolla, a scramble up fixed cables and scree most guidebooks undersell, followed by a long descent into a valley that feels emptied of everyone but marmots.

Cabane de Prafleuri and Cabane des Dix both sit in genuinely wild terrain, glacial and grey, a hard contrast to the flower meadows around Champex-Lac a few days earlier. The Swiss huts serve dinner at a fixed hour and expect payment in cash, so I carried more francs than felt sensible for a hiking trip.

The last two days into Zermatt trade solitude for crowds as you join day-trippers from the Gornergrat, but the payoff is real: the Matterhorn appears and reappears around every ridge for the final thirty kilometres. Go in the first half of September if you can — the passes are usually clear of new snow and the huts have thinned out from the August rush.

article-276.title: The Annapurna Circuit: Nepal's Classic Crossing
article-276.introtext: Nepal's original teahouse trek circles the Annapurna massif over three weeks and one genuinely high pass at 5,416 metres.
article-276.fulltext:
I started in Besisahar and spent the first week gaining altitude gently through Manang district's pine forests and terraced barley fields, sleeping in teahouses that get simpler and colder the higher you climb. By Manang, at 3,500 metres, most groups take a mandatory acclimatisation day, and I used mine to hike up to the Gangapurna glacier viewpoint rather than rest in the lodge.

Thorong La itself is a long, cold, unglamorous slog — a 3am start from High Camp, crampon-worthy ice in places after fresh snow, and a summit that's really just the start of the knee-jarring descent to Muktinath on the other side. What stayed with me was the change in landscape rather than the pass: the wet, green Marsyangdi valley on the eastern approach gives way completely to the high desert of Mustang on the way down.

Buy a walking pole locally in Besisahar or Kathmandu rather than pack one — it's one less thing to carry on the flight, and every teahouse town sells them. Budget more days than the circuit technically requires; altitude sickness sends more trekkers home early than any other single cause, and Manang's acclimatisation day is not optional no matter how good you feel.

article-276.metadesc: Nepal's original teahouse trek circles the Annapurna massif over three weeks and one genuinely high pass at 5,416 metres.

article-277.title: Kamikochi to Yarigatake: A Scramble Through Japan's Northern Alps
article-277.introtext: From the postcard valley of Kamikochi, a two-day scramble leads to the sharpest summit in Japan's Northern Alps.
article-277.fulltext:
Kamikochi itself is almost too civilised to be a trailhead — a valley of clear glacial water and larch forest reachable only by bus, closed to private cars, and busy with day-trippers photographing the Azusa River. I left most of them behind within the first hour, following the river upstream through beech forest before the real climbing starts toward Yarisawa hut.

The final push to Yarigatake's summit is where the trip earns its reputation: a scramble up iron ladders and chains bolted into near-vertical rock, exposed enough that I was glad of the queue slowing everyone to single file at the crux. Mountain huts here run like small hotels, with futons, hot meals and beer for sale, which makes the Japan Alps a strange, comfortable version of high-altitude trekking.

Yarigatake's summit is small and often crowded at sunrise, so I got there the evening before instead and had the ridge nearly to myself. Reserve hut space ahead in peak season, late July to August — Japanese hiking holidays fill Yarisawa and Yarigatake-sanso lodges fast, and turning up without a booking means a long walk back down in the dark.

article-277.metadesc: From the postcard valley of Kamikochi, a two-day scramble leads to the sharpest summit in Japan's Northern Alps.

article-278.title: The Milford Track: Four Days Through Fiordland's Wild Heart
article-278.introtext: Called the finest walk in the world since a Victorian-era journalist coined the phrase, Milford Track still lives up to it across four days through Fiordland.
article-278.fulltext:
Access is tightly controlled — a boat in across Lake Te Anau, a single direction of travel, a fixed number of hikers per day, and three Great Walk huts booked months in advance for the November-to-April season. I crossed Mackinnon Pass on the second morning in a rare clear window, the kind locals say happens on maybe one day in three given Fiordland's rainfall.

The descent off the pass runs beside Sutherland Falls, one of the tallest waterfalls in the country, close enough that the trail gets a fine mist on breezy days. Sandflies are the real hazard here, not weather — I wore repellent from the first hour and still spent an entire evening in a hut common room being quietly eaten alive.

Book through the Department of Conservation the moment the season opens; huts sell out within hours for the popular months. If independent hiking dates don't work, guided trips run the same route with private lodges and hot showers, at several times the price but considerably less logistics.

article-278.metadesc: Called the finest walk in the world since a Victorian-era journalist coined the phrase, Milford Track still lives up to it across four days through Fiordla

article-279.title: The Overland Track: Six Days Across Tasmania's Wilderness
article-279.introtext: Cradle Mountain's jagged dolerite spires mark the start of a six-day traverse across Tasmania's central wilderness to Lake St Clair.
article-279.fulltext:
I picked up the trail at Ronny Creek below Cradle Mountain and Dove Lake, a scene so classically alpine it barely looks Australian, and spent the first afternoon deciding whether to detour up Cradle Mountain's summit itself — most walkers do, weather permitting, since it's a half-day round trip from the main track.

The middle days cross buttongrass moorland and pockets of ancient myrtle-beech rainforest, past Pine Valley and Mt Ossa, Tasmania's highest peak, which I climbed on a side trail from Pelion Plains under a sky that changed four times in an afternoon. Public huts along the route are basic and can fill in peak season, so I carried a tent as backup, which is standard practice here even for people who never end up pitching it.

The track finishes with a choice: walk out along Lake St Clair's shore or take the ferry across, which after six days most people take gladly. Book through the Tasmanian Parks system well ahead for the October-to-May season, when a daily walker cap and mandatory north-to-south direction are both enforced.

article-279.metadesc: Cradle Mountain's jagged dolerite spires mark the start of a six-day traverse across Tasmania's central wilderness to Lake St Clair.

article-280.title: The Toubkal Circuit: Trekking Morocco's High Atlas
article-280.introtext: A loop through Berber villages and high scree slopes in Morocco's High Atlas ends atop North Africa's tallest peak.
article-280.fulltext:
I hired a mule and a guide in Imlil, the trailhead village an hour from Marrakech, which is standard practice here and cheap enough that almost every trekker does the same. The circuit climbs through walnut groves and irrigated terraces before the villages thin out and the trail turns to bare scree above Sidi Chamharouch, a small shrine marking the last real settlement before the mountains close in.

Refuge du Toubkal sits at the base of the final ascent, a functional stone building crowded with trekkers timing their summit push for sunrise. The push to the top of Jbel Toubkal at 4,167 metres is a long, unglamorous scree slog rather than a technical climb, but the altitude and the pre-dawn cold make it feel harder than the numbers suggest.

I came down via the Tizi n'Ougdemt pass rather than retracing my steps, a longer route into the Azzaden valley that trades crowds for empty ridgelines and a last night in a Berber guesthouse. Go in late spring or early autumn — midsummer heat in the lower valleys is brutal, and winter turns the summit push into a genuine mountaineering objective requiring crampons.

article-280.metadesc: A loop through Berber villages and high scree slopes in Morocco's High Atlas ends atop North Africa's tallest peak.

article-281.title: Ciudad Perdida: The Jungle Trek to Colombia's Lost City
article-281.introtext: Four days of dense Sierra Nevada jungle lead to more than a thousand stone terraces built by the Tayrona centuries before the Spanish arrived.
article-281.fulltext:
The trek starts outside Santa Marta and follows the Buritaca River valley through a humidity that never really lets up, crossing the river itself a dozen times on foot and by cable pulley when it's running high. I stayed in open-sided hammock camps each night, mosquito nets included, sharing meals with the same small group of trekkers and indigenous guides for the full four days.

The Kogi and Wiwa communities who still live in the valley are the trek's other half of the story — thatched-roof villages appear along the route, and the guides, several of them Kogi themselves, explain the site's spiritual weight to their own people rather than treating it as a ruin. Ciudad Perdida itself is reached by twelve hundred stone steps cut into the hillside, still slick with moss when I climbed them just after dawn to beat the day-trip crowds arriving by helicopter.

Pack for both heat and rain regardless of season — the valley generates its own weather most afternoons — and bring cash, since there's nowhere to draw money once you leave Santa Marta. Only a handful of licensed agencies run the trek, all following the same route and price band by agreement with the local communities, so choose based on group size rather than itinerary.

article-281.metadesc: Four days of dense Sierra Nevada jungle lead to more than a thousand stone terraces built by the Tayrona centuries before the Spanish arrived.

article-282.title: The Wonderland Trail: Ten Days Circling Mount Rainier
article-282.introtext: The 150-kilometre loop around Mount Rainier crosses more vertical gain than the Grand Canyon rim-to-rim, one river valley and ridge at a time.
article-282.fulltext:
I permitted the trip through the lottery system months ahead, since Wonderland Trail camps are capped and highly competitive for the short July-to-September window when the high passes are reliably clear of snow. The trail circles Rainier at a near-constant middle distance, so the mountain itself is almost always visible, but the terrain underfoot changes completely every few hours — old-growth forest, subalpine meadow, glacial river crossing, scree.

Panhandle Gap, the trail's highest point, still held snow patches when I crossed in early August, and the view stretched south to Mount Adams and, on a clear day, Mount St Helens beyond it. River crossings are the trip's real hazard rather than altitude — the Tahoma and Carbon rivers run high with glacial melt on hot afternoons, and rangers recommend crossing them as early in the day as your itinerary allows.

I carried a bear canister as required and had one uneventful but memorable evening watching a black bear work a huckleberry patch across the valley from camp. Split the trip into ten or eleven days rather than the aggressive seven some parties attempt — the elevation gain adds up fast, and Rainier's weather can close in with little warning even in August.

article-282.metadesc: The 150-kilometre loop around Mount Rainier crosses more vertical gain than the Grand Canyon rim-to-rim, one river valley and ridge at a time.

article-283.title: Zanzibar's Beaches Beyond the Resort Strip
article-283.introtext: On Zanzibar's northeast coast, dhows still outnumber jet skis, and the real tidal rhythm of the Indian Ocean sets the pace of the day.
article-283.fulltext:
Most visitors land at Nungwi or Kendwa, the island's postcard strip of white sand and sunset bars, but the coast keeps going — south past Matemwe's seaweed farms and on to the quieter villages around Pongwe and Michamvi, where the sand is just as fine and the crowds thin to nothing.

Zanzibar's tides swing hard, sometimes three or four meters, so a beach that's lapping at your towel at noon can be a half-mile walk to open water by four; plan swims around the tide chart rather than the clock, and use the low-tide hours to wade out and watch the seaweed farmers working by hand.

Stay in a small guesthouse rather than an all-inclusive resort and you'll eat better for less — grilled octopus and Zanzibar mix from a beachfront stall beats any buffet, and the money stays on the island.
