article-339.metadesc: Solo travel rewards confidence, and confidence is mostly a matter of preparation.

article-340.title: Flying With Toddlers: A Survival Guide for the First Hour
article-340.introtext: The first sixty minutes on board decide the whole flight, so plan for those, not the destination.
article-340.fulltext:
Board last if you can bear the stares in the gate area — every extra minute strapped into a seat is a minute a toddler has to get restless before the plane even moves. Save the new toy, snack or show for the moment the seatbelt sign comes on, not the walk down the jet bridge.

Pack a change of clothes for both of you in the seat-back pocket, not the overhead bin, and bring double the snacks you think you need — turbulence, delays and a refused meal tray can each add an hour you did not budget for. Chewing or sucking through takeoff and landing eases little ears; a bottle, pouch or lollipop works better than any amount of reassurance.

Lower your expectations for screen time on this one trip and no one will remember it in a year. What they will remember, eventually, is the window seat over the Alps or the excitement of a new airport — the tantrum in row 24 fades faster than you think it will.

article-340.metadesc: The first sixty minutes on board decide the whole flight, so plan for those, not the destination.

article-341.title: How to Budget a Three-Month Trip Without a Spreadsheet Meltdown
article-341.introtext: Long trips are won or lost in the planning spreadsheet, but the spreadsheet does not need to be complicated.
article-341.fulltext:
Work out a daily target for food, beds and local transport, then double it for the first week while you calibrate — every destination has a real cost of living, and you will not know yours until you have spent it. After that, track spending weekly rather than daily; daily tracking becomes a chore nobody keeps up.

Book the big-ticket, hard-to-change items — flights, visas, a trekking permit — before you leave, and leave everything else loose. Overplanning a three-month trip wastes the exact flexibility that makes it worth taking three months in the first place.

Build in one splurge a month and one true rest week with no sightseeing at all; both keep budget trips from curdling into endurance tests. The cheapest way to see more of a place is usually to slow down, not speed up — fewer moves, fewer transport costs, fewer wasted travel days.

article-341.metadesc: Long trips are won or lost in the planning spreadsheet, but the spreadsheet does not need to be complicated.

article-342.title: Shoulder Season, Explained: When to Go and Why It Matters
article-342.introtext: The best month to visit almost anywhere is rarely the one everyone else picks.
article-342.fulltext:
Shoulder season sits in the gap between a destination's peak crowds and its harshest weather — often April-May and September-October in the northern hemisphere — when prices soften, queues shrink and locals have time to talk. The trade-off is real: some boat trips stop running, some restaurants close for a break, and daylight hours are shorter.

Check what actually closes before you book, not just what the calendar suggests. A Greek island in early May can be gloriously quiet with half the tavernas still shuttered, so a quick look at opening dates saves a wasted afternoon of walking past locked doors.

Pack for both ends of the weather, since shoulder season swings harder than midsummer — layers earn their keep here more than anywhere. What you get in return is the version of the postcard view without a hundred people in front of it, which is usually worth the gamble.

article-342.metadesc: The best month to visit almost anywhere is rarely the one everyone else picks.

article-343.title: Travel Photography for People Who Don't Own a Real Camera
article-343.introtext: A phone in the right light beats an expensive camera in the wrong one, every time.
article-343.fulltext:
Chase the first and last hour of daylight and skip the flat midday sun altogether; the golden hour does most of the work a camera body never can. If a shot looks dull at noon, it usually is dull at noon — come back at six.

Clean the lens with your shirt before every session; a smudge of pocket lint is the single most common reason a phone photo looks soft. Then get close, get low, or get high — the difference between a snapshot and a photograph is almost always the angle, not the gear.

Shoot the food, the hands, the doorway, not just the wide view everyone else is taking of the same monument. Those small, specific frames are the ones you will actually want to look at again — the landmark shot you can always buy as a postcard.

article-343.metadesc: A phone in the right light beats an expensive camera in the wrong one, every time.

article-344.title: Ten Habits of Genuinely Sustainable Travel
article-344.introtext: Sustainable travel is less about the carbon calculator and more about a handful of habits you carry from trip to trip.
article-344.fulltext:
Take the train or the overnight bus when the distance allows it — the journey becomes part of the trip instead of a cost you endure to reach it, and the emissions saving over short-haul flights is significant. Where flying is unavoidable, fly direct; connections roughly double the footprint of a route.

Spend your money where it stays local: family-run guesthouses over international chains, market stalls over supermarket chains, guides who live in the place you are visiting rather than agencies that fly staff in. It costs about the same and the money actually does something for the place you came to see.

Carry a refillable bottle and a tote, decline the daily towel change, and ask before photographing people, not just landmarks. None of it is dramatic on its own, but a traveller who does all of it leaves a place lighter than they found it, and that is the whole point.

article-344.metadesc: Sustainable travel is less about the carbon calculator and more about a handful of habits you carry from trip to trip.

article-345.title: Copenhagen on Two Wheels: A Long-Weekend Itinerary
article-345.introtext: Denmark's capital makes more sense from a bicycle seat than from any bus tour.
article-345.fulltext:
Rent a bike the moment you land — everyone does, and the city's dedicated lanes make cycling calmer here than walking is in most capitals. Start at Nyhavn's candy-coloured harbour houses first thing, before the tour groups arrive, then pedal along the water to the mermaid statue everyone photographs and few linger at.

Spend an afternoon in Torvehallerne food market for a smorrebrod lunch, then cross into Christianshavn for the crooked spire of Vor Frelsers Kirke and a wander through the loosely-governed streets of Freetown Christiania. Copenhagen rewards an unhurried pace more than a checklist — budget real time for canal-side benches and a coffee that costs more than it should.

Save an evening for Tivoli Gardens, lit up and slightly absurd in the best way, and close the weekend with a swim at one of the harbour baths if the season allows — Copenhageners jump into that water year-round, and a long weekend is exactly long enough to work up the nerve to join them.
article-345.images: {"image_intro":"images\/voyara\/editorial\/copenhagen-long-weekend-cycling.jpg","float_intro":"","image_intro_alt":"The colourful gabled houses and moored wooden boats of Copenhagen's Nyhavn harbour under a blue sky","image_intro_caption":"","image_fulltext":"","float_fulltext":"","image_fulltext_alt":"","image_fulltext_caption":""}
article-345.metadesc: Denmark's capital makes more sense from a bicycle seat than from any bus tour.

article-346.title: Three Days in Prague, Beyond the Charles Bridge Crowds
article-346.introtext: Prague's postcard view is worth the crowd once, but the city gives more to those who look past it.
article-346.fulltext:
Cross the Charles Bridge at sunrise, before the statues disappear behind a wall of selfie sticks, then climb to Prague Castle for the long view back over the red rooftops. The castle complex is bigger than photographs suggest — budget half a day if you want to see St Vitus Cathedral properly rather than glimpse it.

Spend a second day in the Old Town beyond the astronomical clock: the Jewish Quarter's synagogues and old cemetery, then a wander into the winding lanes of Mala Strana where the tour groups thin out fast. A beer in a proper Czech pub — order what the regulars are drinking, not what the menu recommends to tourists — is not optional here; it is closer to a local ritual.

Give the third day to the view from Petrin Hill, reached on foot or by funicular, where Prague spreads out below without a single tour group in the frame. Come down through the Lennon Wall and Kampa Island, and end where you started, on the river, watching the bridge towers go gold at dusk.

article-346.metadesc: Prague's postcard view is worth the crowd once, but the city gives more to those who look past it.

article-347.title: A Weekend in Lisbon: Trams, Tiles and the Tejo
article-347.introtext: Lisbon is a city built on seven hills, and the trams exist for exactly that reason.
article-347.fulltext:
Ride the number 28 tram end to end at least once, ideally early, before the queue for a seat stretches around the block. It rattles through the Alfama's narrow lanes close enough to touch the tiled facades on either side — the best free sightseeing tour the city offers.

Spend a morning getting lost in the Alfama itself on foot, fado drifting out of doorways, then climb to the Miradouro da Senhora do Monte for the widest view over the rooftops down to the Tejo river. Lunch on grilled sardines and a glass of vinho verde somewhere with no view at all — the food is usually better where the tourists are not looking.

Cross to Belem for the custard tarts at the original Pasteis de Belem bakery, still warm and dusted with cinnamon, and the Jeronimos Monastery next door. Close the weekend at a miradouro at sunset with a glass of ginjinha, the sour cherry liqueur sold from tiny hatches all over the old town — Lisbon does its best work in that last hour of light.
article-347.images: {"image_intro":"images\/voyara\/editorial\/weekend-in-lisbon.jpg","float_intro":"","image_intro_alt":"A vintage yellow number 12 tram climbing a narrow street past a whitewashed building in Lisbon's old town","image_intro_caption":"","image_fulltext":"","float_fulltext":"","image_fulltext_alt":"","image_fulltext_caption":""}
article-347.metadesc: Lisbon is a city built on seven hills, and the trams exist for exactly that reason.

article-348.title: Budapest in a Weekend: Thermal Baths and Ruin Bars
article-348.introtext: Budapest runs on hot water and low light, and a weekend here should too.
article-348.fulltext:
Start on the Buda side for the view: Fisherman's Bastion and the Matthias Church at golden hour, with the Danube and the lit-up Parliament building spread out below. Cross the Chain Bridge into Pest as evening falls, when the whole riverfront turns gold and every photograph looks like a postcard.

Spend a morning at the Szechenyi thermal baths, the grand yellow palace of a bathhouse where locals play chess waist-deep in steaming water regardless of the season. Book a slot early on a weekend — Szechenyi gets crowded by midday, and the outdoor pools are worth reaching before the queues do.

After dark, head to the ruin bars of the Jewish Quarter — Szimpla Kert is the famous one, built into a derelict building with mismatched furniture and a courtyard cinema, but the smaller bars on the same streets are worth a wander too. Order a fröccs, the local wine spritzer, and let the night run later than planned; Budapest's best hours often start after most cities have gone quiet.

article-348.metadesc: Budapest runs on hot water and low light, and a weekend here should too.

article-349.title: Valletta: A Long Weekend in Europe's Smallest Capital
article-349.introtext: You can walk across Valletta in twenty minutes, which is exactly why it rewards slowing down.
article-349.fulltext:
Walk in through City Gate and let the grid of honey-coloured limestone streets do the work — every corner reveals another Baroque church facade or a balcony painted the deep green the city is known for. St John's Co-Cathedral looks plain from outside and almost unbelievable within; save an hour for the Caravaggio alone.

Climb to the Upper Barrakka Gardens for the wide view over the Grand Harbour, timed if you can for noon or six, when the saluting battery below fires its cannon in a small daily ceremony that draws a crowd without ever feeling like a show. The harbour itself, still busy with working boats, is what makes Valletta feel lived-in rather than preserved.

Take the short ferry across to the Three Cities for a quieter, less-visited version of the same architecture, then come back for dinner in one of the tiny family-run restaurants tucked into the old town's side streets. Valletta closes early and opens late by Mediterranean standards, so plan meals around a leisurely two-hour lunch rather than a late dinner — the city keeps gentler hours than its neighbours.

article-349.metadesc: You can walk across Valletta in twenty minutes, which is exactly why it rewards slowing down.

article-350.title: Tbilisi Calling: A First-Timer's Long Weekend
article-350.introtext: Georgia's capital is equal parts crumbling and glamorous, and Tbilisi wants you to see both.
article-350.fulltext:
Start in the Old Town below Narikala Fortress, where balconied wooden houses lean into cobbled lanes that smell of fresh bread and grilling meat. Take the cable car up to the fortress itself for the best orientation view of the city, the Kura river curling below and the Bridge of Peace glowing at dusk.

Spend an afternoon in the sulphur bathhouses of Abanotubani, where a scrub-down from a stranger in a private stone chamber is a genuine local institution, not a tourist add-on. Follow it with a proper Georgian supra — a long, wine-soaked feast of khachapuri, khinkali dumplings and endless small plates — and let someone else order, because half the dishes will not be on any menu you recognise.

Ride the funicular up Mtatsminda for sunset over the whole city, then come back down into Fabrika, a converted Soviet factory turned courtyard of bars and independent shops, for a very different Tbilisi after dark. The city rewards curiosity more than any checklist — the best meal of the weekend is usually the one you find by accident, not the one recommended online.
article-350.images: {"image_intro":"images\/voyara\/editorial\/tbilisi-first-timers-weekend.jpg","float_intro":"","image_intro_alt":"The Kura River and a stone bridge in Tbilisi, with the hillside old town and a hilltop church behind","image_intro_caption":"","image_fulltext":"","float_fulltext":"","image_fulltext_alt":"","image_fulltext_caption":""}
article-350.metadesc: Georgia's capital is equal parts crumbling and glamorous, and Tbilisi wants you to see both.

article-351.title: Ljubljana in 48 Hours: Europe's Friendliest Capital
article-351.introtext: Ljubljana is small enough to feel like a village and confident enough to feel like a real capital.
article-351.fulltext:
Start at the Triple Bridge and follow the river through the pedestrianised old town, where outdoor cafes spill onto the banks of the Ljubljanica and dragon statues guard the bridge that gives the city its symbol. The centre is almost entirely car-free, which makes wandering without a map the best strategy the city offers.

Take the funicular up to Ljubljana Castle for a view over the terracotta rooftops to the Julian Alps beyond — on a clear day, Triglav is visible on the horizon, a reminder of how close the mountains sit to this small capital. Come back down for lunch at the Central Market, where farmers sell directly from stalls along the riverbank most mornings.

Cross to Metelkova, a former military barracks turned graffiti-covered arts squat, for a look at a rougher, more improvised Ljubljana after dark. Rent a bike for the second day and ride out to Tivoli Park, the city's green lung, before closing the weekend with a slow dinner by the river — Ljubljana does not rush, and neither should you.

article-351.metadesc: Ljubljana is small enough to feel like a village and confident enough to feel like a real capital.

article-352.title: Seven days on the Trans-Siberian, Moscow to Vladivostok
article-352.introtext: The world's longest railway turns a map into a lived experience, one time zone at a time.
article-352.fulltext:
You board in Moscow with a paper ticket, a compartment number, and roughly nine thousand kilometres ahead of you. The first day is birch forest and provincial stations, the platforms crowded with babushkas selling smoked fish and boiled potatoes through the carriage windows during the longer stops. Time stops mattering in the usual sense — you start living by the train's Moscow-time clock instead of the sun outside.

Compartment life has its own rhythm: glasses of tea in metal holders from the samovar at the end of the carriage, games of cards with whichever nationality you happen to be sharing a cabin with, long silent stretches watching taiga scroll past for hours without a single building. Pack more food than you think you need — the dining car is inconsistent, and the best meals come from platform vendors at Yekaterinburg and Irkutsk.

Break the journey at Lake Baikal — most travellers stop in Irkutsk and take a side trip to Listvyanka or Olkhon Island, where the world's deepest lake sits impossibly blue against the hills. It resets you for the final push through the Russian Far East to Vladivostok, where the railway meets the Pacific and the whole continent-crossing scale of the trip finally lands.

Book a second-class kupe compartment rather than the open-plan platzkart if you want a door that closes, and bring a Russian phrasebook — English thins out fast east of the Urals. The provodnitsa (carriage attendant) runs your world for a week; a friendly relationship with her matters more than any guidebook.

article-352.metadesc: The world's longest railway turns a map into a lived experience, one time zone at a time.

article-353.title: The Gornergrat Railway, Zermatt to the foot of the Matterhorn
article-353.introtext: A cog railway older than the resort it climbs from carries you to one of the great mountain views in the Alps without a single step of walking.
article-353.fulltext:
The train leaves from a small station just behind Zermatt's main street, a red cogwheel carriage that starts climbing almost immediately into larch forest. There is no engine pulling you — a toothed rack under the train grips a matching rail on the track bed, which is how it manages gradients no ordinary train could hold. It has run this way, largely unchanged in principle, since 1898.

The forest thins around Riffelalp and opens into rock and snow, and somewhere past Riffelberg the Matterhorn stops being a postcard and starts filling the window. Sit on the right-hand side going up for the best angle. At Gornergrat itself, 3,089 metres up, you step out onto a viewing terrace surrounded by thirty-eight named peaks over four thousand metres — the Matterhorn, Monte Rosa, the Gorner Glacier spilling down between them.

Go early. The first trains up catch the mountain lit gold before the crowds and before the afternoon cloud that often builds by midday arrives. There is a simple restaurant at the top if you want to linger over coffee with that view rather than rushing back down.

Zermatt itself is car-free, reached only by train from Täsch — so the Gornergrat is really the second act of a journey that starts the moment you leave your car behind. Bring layers regardless of season; the temperature drop between the village and the summit station is dramatic even in July.

article-353.metadesc: A cog railway older than the resort it climbs from carries you to one of the great mountain views in the Alps without a single step of walking.

article-354.title: The slow train to Mount Fuji on the Fujikyuko Line
article-354.introtext: A humble two-car local train out of Otsuki delivers the single best moving view of Japan's sacred mountain.
article-354.fulltext:
Most visitors reach Mount Fuji by bus, which tells you something about how few people know the Fujikyu Railway exists. It's a modest private line running from Otsuki, on the main Chuo route out of Tokyo, up into the lake district around Kawaguchiko — and for the last third of the ride, the mountain simply appears and stays with you, filling the window with almost embarrassing scale.

The carriages are ordinary rather than romantic — vinyl seats, a recorded announcement, commuters getting on and off at small stations along the way — which somehow makes the mountain more startling when it shows up. Sit on the right side heading toward Kawaguchiko for the clearest sightlines, and pick a clear morning; Fuji hides behind haze more often than photographs suggest.

Break the journey at Fujikyu Highland or just ride straight through to Kawaguchiko, where the lake gives you a second, mirrored view of the peak if the wind has dropped. Some of the line's newer trains run oversized picture windows for exactly this stretch — worth checking the timetable for the Fujisan View Express if you want the full cinematic version.

The whole one-way trip from Otsuki runs under an hour and costs a few hundred yen, which makes it one of the cheapest great train rides anywhere. Combine it with a night in Kawaguchiko's onsen ryokan and you get the mountain twice — once from the train, once from the bath.

article-354.metadesc: A humble two-car local train out of Otsuki delivers the single best moving view of Japan's sacred mountain.

article-355.title: Riding the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway's toy train
article-355.introtext: A narrow-gauge steam-era line squeezes between shopfronts and switchbacks its way up nearly two thousand metres to the tea town of Darjeeling.
article-355.fulltext:
The track is barely wider than a garden path — two feet, to be exact — and for long stretches it runs directly down the middle of the Hill Cart Road, so your train shares space with taxis, pedestrians and the occasional cow between New Jalpaiguri and Darjeeling. It has done this since 1881, and UNESCO now protects it as a working World Heritage Site rather than a museum piece.

The signature stretch is the Batasia Loop, where the line spirals over itself to lose height gently enough for the little engines to manage, framing a war memorial with a panorama of Kangchenjunga on a clear morning. Further down, the Agony Point switchback earns its name honestly — the driver reverses the whole train around a hairpin too tight for a normal curve.

Most travellers ride the shorter joyride service from Darjeeling to Ghum, the highest railway station in India, rather than the full seven-hour haul from the plains — it's enough to get the tea-garden views, the diesel-and-steam smell of the old locomotives, and the strange intimacy of a train passing so close to shopfronts you could touch the awnings.

Book the steam-hauled joyride specifically if you can; several services now run modern diesel units instead, which move faster but lose the theatre. Bring a scarf even in summer — Darjeeling sits high enough that mornings stay properly cold.

article-355.metadesc: A narrow-gauge steam-era line squeezes between shopfronts and switchbacks its way up nearly two thousand metres to the tea town of Darjeeling.

article-356.title: The West Highland Line and the curve over Glenfinnan Viaduct
article-356.introtext: Often voted the world's most scenic railway, this line from Fort William to Mallaig crosses lochs, moor and one very famous curved viaduct.
article-356.fulltext:
The regular ScotRail service already justifies the trip on its own — Rannoch Moor's bog and heather stretching to the horizon, Loch Eilt's small wooded islands, the sudden reveal of the sea at Arisaig. But most people come for one specific ninety seconds: the curve of the Glenfinnan Viaduct, twenty-one arches sweeping in a long stone bow above the glen, best known now as the bridge the Hogwarts Express crosses in the Harry Potter films.

You can ride it on the ordinary diurnal train for a fraction of the cost, or take the Jacobite steam service that runs the same route in summer, trailing smoke over the viaduct for the photographers gathered on the hillside viewpoint above Glenfinnan station. Either way, sit on the left heading toward Mallaig for the water views along Loch Shiel and the coast.

Mallaig itself is a working fishing port rather than a tourist set piece — arrive hungry and eat whatever came off the boats that morning, then catch the ferry across to Skye if you want to keep the journey going by water instead of rail.

The full line runs from Glasgow, but the Fort William to Mallaig leg is the concentrated highlight — about ninety minutes each way. Book the Jacobite well ahead in July and August; it sells out weeks in advance.
article-356.images: {"image_intro":"images\/voyara\/editorial\/west-highland-line-glenfinnan-viaduct.jpg","float_intro":"","image_intro_alt":"A steam train crossing the curved multi-arch Glenfinnan Viaduct in the Scottish Highlands, trailing white smoke against hills","image_intro_caption":"","image_fulltext":"","float_fulltext":"","image_fulltext_alt":"","image_fulltext_caption":""}
article-356.metadesc: Often voted the world's most scenic railway, this line from Fort William to Mallaig crosses lochs, moor and one very famous curved viaduct.

article-357.title: The Canadian: four days across a continent by VIA Rail
article-357.introtext: Toronto to Vancouver by transcontinental train trades speed for a slow unspooling of prairie, mountain and lake that no highway or flight can match.
article-357.fulltext:
The Canadian leaves Toronto's Union Station and doesn't really stop being impressive until it reaches the Pacific four days later. The first stretch through Northern Ontario is granite and black spruce and lake after lake, the Canadian Shield at its most repetitive and most hypnotic — you start to understand why this landscape produced a whole school of painters obsessed with exactly this scenery.

Day two brings the Prairies, and this is where the train's slowness becomes the whole point: hour after hour of wheat and canola under a sky too big for any window to properly frame, grain elevators marking small towns from a great distance before the train ever reaches them. The dome cars — glass-topped observation carriages — are worth the upgrade here if nowhere else on the trip.

Then the Rockies arrive almost without warning outside Jasper, and the last day is spent winding through mountain passes and river gorges toward the coast, the scenery changing register completely from the plains. Meals in the dining car are included in sleeper class and run on a fixed schedule that becomes its own kind of ritual — you eat when the train says to eat, and you meet whoever is seated across from you.

Book a cabin rather than coach if your budget allows; four days sitting upright adds up. And bring patience for delays — this is a passenger train sharing freight track, and schedules are treated as more of a suggestion the further west you go.

article-357.metadesc: Toronto to Vancouver by transcontinental train trades speed for a slow unspooling of prairie, mountain and lake that no highway or flight can match.

article-358.title: The Andean Explorer, Cusco to the shores of Lake Titicaca
article-358.introtext: South America's only luxury sleeper train climbs out of the Sacred Valley and across the high Andean plateau to Puno on Lake Titicaca.
article-358.fulltext:
The route leaves Cusco and climbs almost immediately, threading through farming villages where llamas graze alongside the tracks and adobe houses give way to increasingly bare, high-altitude terrain. By the time you reach La Raya pass, you're above 4,300 metres — higher than most Alpine summits — with jagged brown peaks filling the windows and thin cold air that the pressurised carriages handle so smoothly you barely notice.

Meals are served in a dining car with white tablecloths and small lamps at every table, a genuinely incongruous dose of formality against the raw altiplano scenery sliding past outside. There's a piano bar carriage and an open-air observation car at the rear for photographs — worth braving the cold and thin air for, especially as the light goes gold in late afternoon.

The journey ends at Puno on the shore of Lake Titicaca, the highest large navigable lake in the world, where reed islands built by the Uros people float just offshore — a possible extension if you have another day to spare before heading back toward Cusco or on to Bolivia.

The full one-way trip takes about ten hours, so pace yourself with the wine list and the altitude both — even seasoned travellers feel La Raya's thin air. Bring sunglasses; the plateau light at four thousand metres is fierce even through glass.

article-358.metadesc: South America's only luxury sleeper train climbs out of the Sacred Valley and across the high Andean plateau to Puno on Lake Titicaca.

article-359.title: The Flåm Railway, one of the steepest normal-gauge lines on earth
article-359.introtext: Twenty kilometres of switchbacks and waterfalls connect the fjord village of Flåm to the high mountain junction at Myrdal.
article-359.fulltext:
The Flåmsbana climbs 866 metres in under twenty kilometres, a gradient steep enough that the line needed five separate reversing tunnels blasted through solid rock to manage it without switchbacks on the surface. From the fjord-level village of Flåm the train winds up through farmland, then birch forest, then bare mountain, crossing the same valley on different levels so many times that you lose count.

The set-piece stop is Kjosfossen, a thundering waterfall where the train pauses for a few minutes so passengers can get out onto a viewing platform right beside the falls, close enough to feel the spray. In summer a red-clad figure sometimes appears on the rocks above — a nod to local folklore about the huldra, the forest spirits said to lure travellers with song.

At the top, Myrdal connects to the main Oslo–Bergen line, which means you can build a full day out of it: ride the Bergen Railway across the high Hardangervidda plateau, change at Myrdal, and descend the Flåm branch to sea level before catching a fjord cruise onward from the village itself.

Sit on the right-hand side heading down toward Flåm for the best waterfall and valley views. The full descent takes about an hour, and even in July the higher sections can be genuinely cold — pack a proper layer, not just a cardigan.

article-359.metadesc: Twenty kilometres of switchbacks and waterfalls connect the fjord village of Flåm to the high mountain junction at Myrdal.

article-360.title: Kandy to Ella through Sri Lanka's tea country
article-360.introtext: Sri Lanka's hill-country line climbs through terraced tea gardens and over the famous Nine Arch Bridge on its way to the cool town of Ella.
article-360.fulltext:
The train from Kandy climbs almost from the first mile, leaving the humid lowlands behind for a cooler, greener world of tea estates that carpet every hillside in tight, geometric rows. Pickers in bright saris move between the bushes as the train passes, and the smell of processing sheds drifts through open windows at stations like Nanu Oya, the stop for Nuwara Eliya.

Doors are left open for the whole ride, which is technically against the rules and practically the entire point — passengers lean out or sit in the doorway with legs dangling as the carriages sway through curve after curve. Second and third class are where the real atmosphere lives; the reserved first-class observation car is comfortable but oddly sealed off from the experience everyone comes for.

The line's postcard moment is the Nine Arch Bridge outside Ella, a colonial-era viaduct built without steel — legend says its engineer used only brick, cement and railway track after wartime steel shortages — now framed by jungle and tea slopes on every side. Get off a stop early at Demodara and walk to the bridge for photos before continuing on to Ella itself.

Book second class in advance through the official reservation system if you want a guaranteed seat — this route has become popular enough that unreserved carriages fill early. The full Kandy–Ella run takes six to seven hours; treat it as the destination, not the commute.

article-360.metadesc: Sri Lanka's hill-country line climbs through terraced tea gardens and over the famous Nine Arch Bridge on its way to the cool town of Ella.

article-361.title: The Ghan: three days through Australia's red centre
article-361.introtext: Named for the Afghan cameleers who once opened this route, the Ghan crosses an entire continent from Adelaide to Darwin through country few travellers ever see.
article-361.fulltext:
The journey covers nearly three thousand kilometres of the emptiest interior on the planet — scrub, then desert, then the sudden deep red of the Simpson Desert's dune country, then finally tropical green as you approach the Top End. Old rusted locomotives and abandoned sidings from the original narrow-gauge line still sit out in the desert near towns like Marree, remnants of the route's much harder early history before the modern standard-gauge line replaced it in 2004.

Off-train excursions are built into the ticket and are where the trip really opens up: a sunset walk through the West MacDonnell Ranges outside Alice Springs, a visit to Katherine Gorge further north, or simply time in the small town of Alice Springs itself, roughly the halfway point and the only real settlement the route passes through for hundreds of kilometres in either direction.

Onboard, the days settle into a rhythm of dining car meals, a lounge car with a well-stocked bar, and long unbroken hours watching country scroll past that changes almost imperceptibly hour to hour but transforms completely over the length of the journey. Cabins are small but proper beds, not couchettes, which matters over three days.

Book well ahead — the Ghan operates on a fixed seasonal schedule rather than daily departures, running more frequently between April and November. The heat further north can be extreme even in the shoulder months, so factor that into what you pack for the excursions.

article-362.title: Watching the wildebeest brave the Mara River
article-362.introtext: Nothing in East Africa matches the noise and nerve of a wildebeest column throwing itself into the crocodile-thick Mara River at the height of the migration.
article-362.fulltext:
By late July the herds have massed on the Serengeti bank in their thousands, bellowing and pacing for hours before a single animal finally commits. Once the first wildebeest goes, the whole column follows in a scrambling, dust-choked rush, hooves drumming on mud and rock as zebras thread through the chaos alongside them.

The crossing itself lasts only minutes but it is total sensory overload: the crack of horns against horns, the slap of bodies hitting water, a crocodile surfacing exactly where you did not expect one. Guides cut the engine and let the vehicle drift into position well before the herd commits, because once it starts there is no repositioning without spooking the animals mid-crossing.

Base yourself on the Kenyan side of the Mara Triangle or the northern Serengeti between late July and September, when the migration is most likely to be pinned against the river. Pack a long lens and patience in equal measure — some mornings you wait four hours for a crossing that never comes, and that is simply the honest rhythm of following a wild herd.

article-363.title: Tracking jaguars by boat in the Brazilian Pantanal
article-363.introtext: The Pantanal's flooded rivers hold the best odds on Earth of watching a wild jaguar hunt in daylight, from the low seat of a skiff.
article-363.fulltext:
Unlike the Amazon's dense canopy, the Pantanal's open wetlands and clear sightlines mean jaguars here hunt caiman and capybara along exposed riverbanks in full view of a boat. Spotters radio between skiffs along the Rio Cuiabá and Três Irmãos, so a sighting anywhere on the water usually pulls two or three boats into a respectful, engine-off arc within minutes.

You come to recognise the tells before the cat itself appears: a line of birds lifting off a bank in alarm, capybara freezing mid-graze, or simply your guide cutting speed and pointing at a patch of shade that looks, at first, like nothing at all. When a jaguar does step down to drink, it moves with an unhurried confidence that makes the whole boatload go silent at once.

Go in the dry season, June through October, when falling water levels concentrate prey and cats alike along the exposed banks and the dirt access road, the Transpantaneira, is passable end to end. Stay at a fazenda lodge with its own boats rather than a day-tripping operator — the earlier starts and later returns are where the best sightings happen.

article-364.title: Drifting past orangutans on the Kinabatangan River
article-364.introtext: A slow boat along Sabah's Kinabatangan River turns up more wild orangutans in an afternoon than most people see in a lifetime of nature documentaries.
article-364.fulltext:
The river cuts through one of the last stretches of lowland rainforest on Borneo, and its banks concentrate wildlife the way a waterhole does on the savanna. Twice a day, at dawn and again as the light goes gold before dusk, flat-bottomed boats nose along the water while guides scan the canopy for a telltale shiver of branches.

Orangutans move through the trees with a slow, deliberate grace, often a mother with an infant clinging to her flank, and it is common to drift beneath a fig tree and simply watch one feed for twenty unhurried minutes. Proboscis monkeys, hornbills and, if you are fortunate, a pygmy elephant herd wading through the shallows round out a single cruise.

Base yourself in Sukau or Bilit rather than day-tripping from Sandakan, since a lodge on the river gets you onto the water for both golden-hour cruises instead of just one. Bring a dry bag for anything electronic — afternoon squalls arrive fast and the boats have no real cover.

article-364.metadesc: A slow boat along Sabah's Kinabatangan River turns up more wild orangutans in an afternoon than most people see in a lifetime of nature documentaries.

article-365.title: Blue feet and no fear: wildlife encounters in the Galápagos
article-365.introtext: The Galápagos is the rare place where wild animals simply ignore you, letting you sit an arm's length from a blue-footed booby without it so much as breaking stride.
article-365.fulltext:
Charles Darwin's finches get the credit, but it is the tameness of everything here that actually stuns first-time visitors. Sea lions nap across footpaths and beaches without moving for passing boots, marine iguanas pile onto black lava rock in stacks of a dozen, and blue-footed boobies perform their high-stepping courtship dance a few feet from where you stand.

Every island specialises in something different, which is why island-hopping beats staying put: Española for the extraordinary tameness of its birdlife, North Seymour for frigatebirds with scarlet throat pouches inflated like balloons, and the highlands of Santa Cruz for giant tortoises grazing in the wild. Snorkelling adds a second layer entirely — sea lions loop and dart around swimmers with an almost puppyish curiosity.

Book through a licensed operator with a fixed itinerary, since the national park strictly regulates which sites each boat may visit and when, and pack reef-safe sunscreen — nothing else is permitted in the water here. Visit between June and December for cooler water, better snorkelling visibility and albatross courtship on Española.

article-366.title: Jeep safaris among Kaziranga's one-horned rhinos
article-366.introtext: Kaziranga's tall elephant grass and Brahmaputra floodplain hold two-thirds of the world's greater one-horned rhinos, a conservation story you can watch unfold from an open jeep at dawn.
article-366.fulltext:
Assam's grasslands look almost prehistoric at first light, mist lifting off the swamp as a rhino's armoured grey bulk emerges from the reeds to graze. The species was hunted to a few hundred animals last century; today Kaziranga alone holds over two thousand, grazing alongside wild water buffalo, swamp deer and, if you are lucky, a tiger crossing the track ahead of the jeep.

The park is split into ranges — Central, Western, Eastern and Burapahar — and each has a different character, from open floodplain to denser forest edge, so a two-day visit covering more than one range is worth the extra permit. Early starts matter enormously here: the grass is at its shortest and the animals most active in the hour after the gates open.

Kaziranga closes entirely during the monsoon floods, so plan a visit between November and April when the park is dry and accessible. Add an elephant-back safari for a different vantage into grass too tall to see over from a jeep, though book it the evening before — slots fill fast in peak season.

article-367.title: Tundra buggies and polar bears on the shores of Hudson Bay
article-367.introtext: Every October, polar bears converge on the shoreline near Churchill, Manitoba, to wait out the days until Hudson Bay freezes solid enough to hunt seals again.
article-367.fulltext:
The town styles itself the polar bear capital of the world, and for a few weeks each autumn that is no exaggeration — bears wander through the willow scrub in numbers found nowhere else, drawn to this exact stretch of coast by currents that freeze the bay here first. Elevated tundra buggies with viewing decks let you watch from a safe height as bears spar, doze in the low sun, or approach the vehicle out of sheer curiosity.

What surprises most visitors is how much personality comes through at close range: a mother cuffing a stubborn cub back into line, two young males play-fighting on their hind legs, the particular unhurried roll of a bear settling down to sleep on frozen ground. Temperatures swing brutally even at midday, so the buggies' heated cabins are not a luxury but a necessity.

Fly into Churchill via Winnipeg — there is no road connection — and book buggy tours well ahead, since operators cap numbers and the best late-October and early-November dates sell out a year in advance. Layer aggressively: parka, insulated boots and mitts rated well below what the forecast suggests, because wind off the bay cuts through anything less.

article-368.title: Chasing the resplendent quetzal above San Gerardo de Dota
article-368.introtext: The resplendent quetzal's iridescent tail and improbable colouring have drawn birders to Costa Rica's high cloud forest for decades, and the valley of San Gerardo de Dota remains the surest place to find one.
article-368.fulltext:
At nearly 2,300 metres in the Talamanca mountains, the air turns cool and the forest closes into a dripping tangle of oaks draped in moss and bromeliads. Quetzals nest in these hollow oak trunks and feed on wild avocado, so local guides know the fruiting trees by heart and can often position a group beneath one before the bird even shows.

The reveal, when it comes, still stops conversation: a flash of iridescent green and crimson, then that absurdly long tail streaming behind as the bird settles on a branch to swallow a fruit whole. Mixed flocks of tanagers and trogons move through the same canopy, so the wait between quetzal sightings is rarely dull.

Go between January and April, the local dry season and also nesting time, when quetzals are most reliably active around their chosen trees in the early morning. Book a guide the evening before rather than wandering alone — their knowledge of which specific tree is fruiting that week is the difference between an hour's wait and a full morning's search.

article-369.title: Among a quarter-million king penguins at South Georgia's Gold Harbour
article-369.introtext: Nothing prepares you for Gold Harbour — a beach on South Georgia so densely packed with king penguins that the shoreline itself seems to move.
article-369.fulltext:
Expedition ships anchor offshore and ferry passengers in by zodiac, and the noise reaches you before the beach does: a constant trumpeting chorus from tens of thousands of adults, chicks and moulting juveniles in their shaggy brown down. Snow-capped peaks and a hanging glacier frame the colony, so the scale only really registers once you are standing at the edge of it, penguins stretching to the horizon in both directions.

Strict biosecurity rules keep visitors at a set distance from the birds, though the penguins themselves have no such boundaries and will happily waddle right up to inspect your boots. Elephant seals wallow in the shallows nearby, and fur seal pups patrol the tussock grass with more attitude than their size suggests they should have.

South Georgia is reached only by expedition ship, usually as an add-on to an Antarctic Peninsula voyage departing Ushuaia, with landings weather-dependent and never guaranteed in advance. Wear layered waterproofs rather than a single heavy coat — zodiac landings mean wet feet and spray regardless of season, and the weather can shift within the hour.

article-370.title: Leopard spotting in the scrub of Yala National Park
article-370.introtext: Yala holds one of the highest densities of leopards anywhere on the planet, and unlike most big-cat destinations, here the odds of a sighting genuinely favour you.
article-370.fulltext:
The park's dry scrub and rocky outcrops give leopards clear vantage points to survey their territory, and with no larger predator to compete against, they hunt and rest in the open with a confidence rarely seen elsewhere. A jeep convoy easing to a stop, radios crackling between drivers, is usually the first sign that a cat has been spotted lounging on a boulder or padding along a trail.

What makes Yala's leopards so watchable is their sheer indifference to vehicles — a cat will often walk straight past a line of jeeps, close enough to see the individual rosettes in its coat, without breaking stride. Elephants, sloth bears and a huge diversity of waterbirds fill the gaps between leopard sightings, so even a quiet game drive rarely feels empty.

Block 1, nearest the entrance, has the highest leopard density but also the heaviest jeep traffic in peak season; consider Block 5 or a private reserve on the park's boundary for a quieter, less crowded safari. Visit in the dry season from February to July, when receding waterholes concentrate both predators and prey along predictable routes.

article-371.title: Gliding by mokoro through the Okavango Delta
article-371.introtext: The Okavango Delta is a rare inland river that never reaches the sea, and the quietest way to experience it is from a hand-poled mokoro sliding silently between the reeds.
article-371.fulltext:
Water flooding down from Angolan highlands spreads across the Kalahari sands each year, transforming dry bush into a maze of lagoons and channels that draws game from across northern Botswana. A mokoro poler standing at the stern reads the water with a practised eye, easing the canoe past lily pads and papyrus with barely a ripple, so animals rarely register your approach until you are already close.

Elephants wade and swim between islands with only trunks and backs breaking the surface, hippos surface and submerge in the deeper channels, and red lechwe bound through the shallows in explosive leaps when startled. The silence of a mokoro compared to a vehicle changes the whole texture of a sighting — you hear the water move before you see what caused it.

The flood typically peaks between June and August, when water levels are highest and mokoro access opens up further into the delta's interior; drier months favour game drives instead as channels shrink. Choose a camp with both mokoro and vehicle safaris on offer so you are not locked into one mode of travel regardless of that week's water levels.

article-372.title: Okavango Delta Mokoro Safari
article-372.introtext: Glide silently through papyrus channels by dugout canoe and track big game on foot in one of Africa's last true wildernesses.
article-372.fulltext:
The Okavango Delta is Africa's great paradox: a river that never reaches the sea, fanning out across the Kalahari into a maze of lagoons, palm islands and floodplains that swell each year with floodwater from the Angolan highlands. This trip puts you at the heart of it, based at classic tented camps reachable only by light aircraft, where elephant and buffalo wade past your deck and the days move at the pace of the water itself.

Mornings are spent gliding between reed channels in a mokoro, poled by a local guide who reads the delta like a map, spotting red lechwe, fish eagles and the occasional submerged hippo before you've seen a ripple. Afternoons switch to open 4x4 game drives and walking safaris on the drier islands, tracking lion and wild dog with guides who grew up in these channels. It suits travellers who want their Africa unhurried, intimate and genuinely remote.

article-373.title: Volcanoes Gorilla Trek and Kigali
article-373.introtext: Trek the bamboo slopes of the Virunga volcanoes to spend an hour with mountain gorillas, framed by Kigali's hills and hospitality.
article-373.fulltext:
Rwanda has turned itself into one of the world's great conservation stories, and nowhere shows it better than Volcanoes National Park, where more than a dozen habituated gorilla families roam the forested slopes of the Virungas. This trip opens in Kigali, a green, orderly hillside capital worth two full days on its own, before heading north to Musanze for guided treks through bamboo and stinging nettle to sit, in near silence, a few metres from a family of mountain gorillas.

Trekking difficulty varies daily depending on which family you're assigned, so mornings begin with a briefing and a walking stick, and the climb itself can run from ninety minutes to four hours each way. Beyond the primary gorilla trek, the itinerary adds a golden monkey excursion in the bamboo forest and a community visit in a Virunga foothill village, giving a fuller picture of a country that has rebuilt itself around its wildlife and its people.

article-374.title: Nile Cruise: Luxor to Aswan
article-374.introtext: Sail the classic river route between Luxor and Aswan, waking each morning to a new temple on the Nile's banks.
article-374.fulltext:
This is the Nile journey travellers have taken for two centuries, and it still delivers: a small, traditionally rigged cruise boat drifting between Luxor and Aswan, stopping at Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, Edfu and Kom Ombo along the way. Days alternate between guided temple visits at dawn, when the stone is cool and the crowds thin, and slow afternoons on deck watching palm-lined riverbanks and village life slide past.

Evenings bring felucca sails at sunset and dinners on deck under Aswan's clearer, desert-edged sky, before a final excursion by road to Abu Simbel. The pace is unhurried by design, built for travellers who want Egypt's ancient sites explained properly by an Egyptologist guide rather than rushed through, with the river itself doing most of the transporting.

article-375.title: Sossusvlei Dunes and Deadvlei
article-375.introtext: Climb the world's tallest red dunes and stand among the fossilised camel thorn trees of Deadvlei at first light.
article-375.fulltext:
The Namib is the oldest desert on Earth, and Sossusvlei is its centrepiece: a sea of star-shaped dunes, some over 300 metres high, glowing deep orange against a hard blue sky. This short, focused trip is built around getting you onto the dunes and into Deadvlei's cracked white clay pan before sunrise, when the light is at its sharpest and the tour buses haven't yet arrived, then giving the desert room to breathe for the rest of each day.

Beyond the dunes themselves, the itinerary threads through Sesriem Canyon's slot walls and out to the wild Atlantic coast at Swakopmund, taking in the seal colonies and shipwreck-strewn Skeleton Coast along the way. Distances are long and the roads are gravel, so this suits travellers happy to trade pavement for scenery and to rise before dawn for the reward of an empty dune ridge.

article-376.title: Inca Trail to Machu Picchu
article-376.introtext: Walk the classic four-day Inca Trail through cloud forest and stone gateways to reach Machu Picchu at first light.
article-376.fulltext:
The Inca Trail is the original approach to Machu Picchu, and still the best. This is the classic 43-kilometre route the Incas built, threading past ruins at Llaqtapata and Wiñay Wayna, over the 4,215-metre Dead Woman's Pass, and down through cloud forest to the Sun Gate for a first sunrise view of the citadel below. It suits fit walkers who want the payoff of arriving on foot rather than by train.

You'll camp three nights with a full support crew — porters, cook, and an English-speaking guide who threads the history of the Inca road system through each day's walk. Group size is capped and permits are limited, so trail dates fill early. The reward is arriving at Machu Picchu through the Sun Gate at dawn, ahead of the day-trip crowds, with the citadel and Huayna Picchu unfolding in the early light exactly as Hiram Bingham first saw it in 1911.

article-377.title: Patagonia: Fitz Roy Trek in El Chaltén
article-377.introtext: Trek beneath the granite spires of Fitz Roy in Argentina's trekking capital, El Chaltén.
article-377.fulltext:
El Chaltén sits at the base of Cerro Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre, twin granite towers that draw climbers and walkers from across the world. This trip bases you in the village for four nights and covers the region's signature trails on foot — no technical climbing required, just sustained day-hiking on well-marked Los Glaciares National Park trails with a guide who knows which viewpoints catch the peaks clear of cloud.

Highlights include the hike to Laguna de los Tres, where Fitz Roy rises directly above a glacial lake, and the quieter Laguna Torre trail beneath Cerro Torre's needle spire. Weather here changes fast — Patagonia's wind and light are part of the experience — and your guide builds flexibility into the itinerary to chase clear-sky windows. Evenings are spent in El Chaltén's small restaurants over Malbec and Patagonian lamb, planning the next day around the forecast.

article-378.title: Bolivia: Uyuni Salt Flats and Altiplano
article-378.introtext: Cross the world's largest salt flat by 4x4 and climb into the high-desert Altiplano's coloured lagoons.
article-378.fulltext:
Salar de Uyuni is 10,000 square kilometres of blinding white salt crust, and after rain it turns into the world's largest mirror, doubling the sky underfoot. This overland trip crosses the salar by 4x4 with a local driver-guide, stopping at the cactus-covered Isla Incahuasi and the old train cemetery outside Uyuni town, before climbing into the Altiplano's volcanic backcountry.

Beyond the salt flat, the route runs through Eduardo Avaroa National Reserve — red and green lagoons stained by algae and minerals, flamingo colonies at 4,500 metres, geysers venting at dawn, and the Dalí Desert's wind-sculpted rock formations. Nights are spent in simple salt-brick and stone lodges at altitude; the cold is real, but the star-filled skies over the salar are unlike anywhere else on the trip circuit.

article-379.title: Galápagos Islands Small-Ship Cruise
article-379.introtext: Cruise the Galápagos archipelago by small ship, snorkeling and hiking among wildlife that has never learned to fear people.
article-379.fulltext:
The Galápagos are best seen by boat, moving between islands overnight so each morning opens on a different landscape and species mix. This trip runs aboard a small first-class catamaran carrying under twenty guests, with a certified naturalist guide leading every landing under National Park permit. You'll walk among giant tortoises, sea lion colonies, marine iguanas and blue-footed boobies that show no instinct to flee — Darwin's living laboratory, largely unchanged.

Days alternate between dry landings on volcanic trails and wet landings onto white- and black-sand beaches, with snorkeling most afternoons alongside sea turtles, rays and reef sharks in startlingly clear water. The itinerary covers both the central islands — Santa Cruz, North Seymour, Bartolomé — and outer islands with their own endemic species, giving a fuller picture of the archipelago than any single-island stay could.

article-380.title: Colombia's Coffee Triangle and Cocora Valley
article-380.introtext: Ride, hike and sip your way through Colombia's Zona Cafetera, from working coffee farms to the towering wax palms of Cocora Valley.
article-380.fulltext:
Colombia's Eje Cafetero produces some of the world's best arabica, grown on steep volcanic hillsides between Salento, Filandia and Manizales. This trip is based in small fincas and colourful pueblo hotels, with mornings spent on working coffee farms learning the process from cherry to cup, and afternoons exploring the region's postcard towns with their balconied wooden houses and central plazas.

The centerpiece is a day in Cocora Valley, home to the wax palm — Colombia's national tree and the tallest palm species on earth — hiking through cloud forest and open pasture where the palms rise 60 metres against the mist. Add horseback rides through coffee country, a visit to the Panchina thermal springs, and evenings over tinto and aguardiente in Salento's plaza, and you get a slower, deeply local read on Colombia far from the coastal resorts.

article-381.title: Canadian Rockies: Icefields Parkway Road Journey
article-381.introtext: Drive one of the world's most scenic highways past turquoise lakes, glaciers and snow-capped peaks between Banff and Jasper.
article-381.fulltext:
The Icefields Parkway links Banff and Jasper national parks along 230 kilometres of continuous mountain scenery — glacier-fed lakes in impossible shades of blue, hanging glaciers visible from the road, and wildlife that regularly includes elk, bighorn sheep and the odd black bear along the verges. This self-drive trip is built around short, well-placed stops rather than long driving days, with a private vehicle and driver-guide so you're never rushing between viewpoints.

Anchor stops include Moraine Lake and Lake Louise at dawn before the crowds arrive, the Columbia Icefield with its own walkable glacier tongue, and Peyto Lake's wolf-head-shaped bay from the Bow Summit viewpoint. Short hikes fill the afternoons — Johnston Canyon's waterfalls, the Wilcox Pass ridge walk facing the icefield — and nights are spent in Banff, Lake Louise and Jasper townsite, with mountain-view rooms wherever the route allows.

article-382.title: Everest Base Camp Trek
article-382.introtext: Walk the Khumbu valley trail beneath the world's highest peaks to stand at the foot of Everest itself.
article-382.fulltext:
This is the trek every mountain walker dreams about: fourteen days through Sherpa country, from the roaring airstrip at Lukla up through pine forest, suspension bridges strung with prayer flags, and the trading town of Namche Bazaar, to the ice and rock of the Khumbu glacier. You gain altitude the way you're supposed to — slowly, with acclimatisation days built in at Namche and Dingboche — so your body has a fair chance to adjust before you sleep at nearly 5,000 metres.

The reward is not one view but a fortnight of them: Ama Dablam's fluted spire, the monastery at Tengboche with its backdrop of Everest and Lhotse, and finally the boulder field at Base Camp itself, tents dwarfed by the Khumbu Icefall. Most trekkers add the dawn climb to Kala Patthar for the classic Everest panorama. You'll sleep in family-run lodges the whole way, eating dal bhat and drinking incredibly sweet milk tea, guided by Sherpa staff who know this trail like their own front yard — because for many of them, it is.

article-383.title: Annapurna Circuit and Poon Hill Panorama
article-383.introtext: Cross a Himalayan pass above 5,000 metres and drop into the Kali Gandaki, the deepest gorge on Earth.
article-383.fulltext:
The Annapurna Circuit is the classic long trek of Nepal: sixteen days that carry you from subtropical rice terraces around Pokhara, up through pine and rhododendron forest, past yak pastures and mani walls, to the wind-scoured Thorong La pass at 5,416 metres. On the far side, the trail drops into Mustang's rain-shadow desert and the Kali Gandaki gorge, before threading back through Gurung and Thakali villages with sweeping views of Annapurna, Dhaulagiri and Machapuchare's unmistakable fishtail summit.

Unlike the single-valley Everest routes, the Circuit changes character daily — you'll walk through half a dozen distinct climate zones and as many ethnic regions in the space of two weeks. Nights are spent in stone-built teahouses run by the same families for generations, and the route finishes with a side trip to Poon Hill for one of the most photographed sunrises in the world. It's demanding at altitude but doesn't require technical skill, making it the trek serious hikers choose for variety over any single dramatic peak.

article-384.title: Bhutan Druk Path Trek and Paro Cultural Journey
article-384.introtext: Trek between hidden mountain lakes on the trail that once linked Bhutan's two great valleys, then descend to the cliffside Tiger's Nest.
article-384.fulltext:
The Druk Path is a short, spectacular trek in the last Buddhist kingdom in the Himalaya, following the old trading route between Paro and Thimphu over a string of high alpine lakes ringed by rhododendron forest. Camps are set beside water at 3,800–4,200 metres, with clear views to Jomolhari and the Bhutanese high country on good days. Because Bhutan caps its visitor numbers and requires a licensed guide throughout, the trails feel remarkably uncrowded — you're more likely to meet a yak herder than another trekking group.

We bookend the trek with cultural days in Paro and Thimphu: the fortress-monastery (dzong) at Paro, the National Museum, and archery matches in the capital. The trip closes with the hike to Paro Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest monastery, glued to a cliff 900 metres above the valley floor — arguably the single most photographed building in the Himalaya, and worth every step of the climb.

article-385.title: Ladakh Markha Valley Trek
article-385.introtext: Trek Ladakh's classic high desert valley, past whitewashed gompas and over the Kongmaru La, in the shadow of the Zanskar range.
article-385.fulltext:
Ladakh sits in the rain shadow of the Himalaya, and the Markha Valley trek shows off the result: bare ochre mountains, a ribbon of barley fields and poplar trees along the river, and Buddhist monasteries perched on outcrops that look painted onto the landscape. The route follows the Markha river through the villages of Skiu, Markha and Hankar inside Hemis National Park — snow leopard country, though you're far more likely to spot herds of blue sheep than the cats themselves — before climbing to the Kongmaru La at 5,150 metres for a final panorama of the Zanskar and Ladakh ranges.

This is trekking with a strong cultural thread: you'll stay in village homestays as often as tents, share butter tea with Ladakhi families, and visit the cliffside gompa at Hankar and the royal fort ruins above the valley. Leh itself, with its own palace and old town, makes an atmospheric start and end point, and we build in a full acclimatisation day there before setting off — Ladakh's altitude catches out anyone who rushes it.

article-386.title: Kyrgyzstan Tian Shan and Song-Kol Lake Trek
article-386.introtext: Ride and hike through Kyrgyzstan's high summer pastures to camp in a nomad's yurt beside alpine Song-Kol lake.
article-386.fulltext:
Kyrgyzstan is where Central Asia's nomadic tradition is still a living, working culture rather than a museum piece, and this trip is built around that fact. From Bishkek we head into the Tian Shan — the 'Celestial Mountains' — walking and riding through the Suusamyr and Kok-Jайык valleys where families still move their herds to jailoo summer pasture every June. The route climbs gradually to Song-Kol, a vast alpine lake at 3,000 metres ringed by open grassland, where we sleep two nights in a traditional felt yurt camp run by a local family.

Days are a mix of hiking, horse-trekking and simple camp life: milking mares for kumis, watching eagle hunters demonstrate their birds, and sharing bread and jam around a wood stove in the evening. It's a gentler physical challenge than the high Himalaya treks in this collection, but the scale of the empty green landscape — and the warmth of Kyrgyz hospitality — leaves an equally strong impression.

article-387.title: Tajikistan Pamir Highway Overland Journey
article-387.introtext: Drive the world's second-highest international highway across the Pamir plateau, from turquoise mountain lakes to the Wakhan Corridor.
article-387.fulltext:
The Pamir Highway (the M41) is one of the great overland drives on Earth, climbing from Dushanbe's poplar-lined streets into the 'Roof of the World' — a high plateau of 6,000-metre peaks, salt lakes and wind-scoured passes that has barely changed since it was a branch of the Silk Road. We travel it in stages by 4x4, with time to stop: the turquoise reservoir at Iskanderkul in the Fann Mountains, the hot springs and Pamiri villages of the Wakhan Corridor within sight of Afghanistan, and the wild high-altitude lakes around Bulunkul and Yashilkul.

This is a trip for travellers who want landscape and culture over strenuous hiking — days involve short walks to viewpoints and villages rather than long treks, with most distance covered by vehicle on rough but spectacular roads. Nights are spent in family homestays wherever possible, where Pamiri hospitality is legendary: you'll be fed more bread, tea and apricot jam than you can manage, often by women in the region's distinctive embroidered headscarves, at gatherings that double as the trip's best cultural memories.

article-388.title: Almaty and the Trans-Ili Alatau Mountains
article-388.introtext: A short, scenic escape into the snow-capped range that rises straight out of Kazakhstan's greenest city.
article-388.fulltext:
Almaty is unusual among big cities in having genuine high mountains at its back door — the Trans-Ili Alatau range climbs to over 4,000 metres barely half an hour from downtown. This trip uses the city as a comfortable base for day hikes and cable-car rides into that range: the ski slopes and viewpoints of Shymbulak, the glacial cirque at Big Almaty Lake, and a full-day excursion to the turquoise Kolsai Lakes further east, often called the 'Pearl of the Tian Shan.'

It's the easiest trip in our Central Asia collection, built for travellers who want big alpine scenery without multi-day trekking commitment — most days combine a moderate walk with a chairlift or vehicle for the harder climbing. Evenings are spent back in Almaty's leafy streets, sampling Kazakh and Uyghur cuisine and browsing the Central State Museum, making this a good add-on before or after a longer Central Asian trek.

article-389.title: Kiso Valley Post Towns: Narai to Nezame-no-Toko
article-389.introtext: A quieter stretch of the old Nakasendo — the lacquerware town of Narai, the Torii Pass, and the granite gorge of Nezame-no-Toko — walked at an unhurried pace.
article-389.fulltext:
While most visitors to the Kiso Valley stop at Magome and Tsumago, the post towns further north see a fraction of the crowds and lose none of the atmosphere. This trip follows the Nakasendo from Narai-juku — the longest of the valley's 11 post towns, its single street lined with lacquerware workshops and combware makers — up over the forested Torii Pass to Yabuhara, then on by local train and foot to the river-carved rock formations at Nezame-no-Toko.

It's a trip for travellers who want the Edo-period atmosphere of the Kiso Valley without the tour-bus crowds, plenty of time in family-run inns, and short, well-marked walking days through cedar forest and river gorge. Evenings are spent in minshuku and small ryokan eating hoba miso and mountain vegetables, with the Kiso River running past almost every window.

article-390.title: Walking the Shikoku 88-Temple Pilgrim Trail
article-390.introtext: A guided introduction to Japan's great henro pilgrimage — walking sections of the 1,200-kilometre route between temples founded by Kobo Daishi.
article-390.fulltext:
The Shikoku pilgrimage links 88 temples in a loop around the island, traditionally walked in white robes with a wooden staff over 40 days or more. This trip does not attempt the full circuit — instead it walks the most rewarding sections in the Tokushima and Kochi prefectures, riding between distant clusters so the days on foot are spent on genuine pilgrim paths rather than roadside shoulders.

You'll stay in temple lodgings and family-run pilgrim inns, ring bells at torii-flanked shrines shared between Buddhist and Shinto practice, and eat with fellow walkers — Japanese and foreign — who are on their own version of the same journey. It suits travellers drawn to Japan's spiritual side and comfortable with unhurried, repetitive walking days.

article-391.title: Kamikochi and the Northern Japan Alps
article-391.introtext: A high-alpine trek through Kamikochi's protected valley and the jagged peaks of the Hotaka range, Japan's most dramatic mountain scenery.
article-391.fulltext:
Kamikochi is a car-free valley 1,500 metres up in the Northern Japan Alps, ringed by the serrated Hotaka peaks and threaded by the clear Azusa River. This trek uses it as a base for progressively longer days — gentle valley walks past the iconic Kappa-bashi bridge at first, building to a full mountain-hut crossing toward Mount Yarigatake for those with alpine experience.

Days start early to catch the peaks before cloud builds, and evenings are spent in mountain lodges or a riverside ryokan with an outdoor onsen. Autumn brings golden larch and crowds; early summer brings snow patches still clinging to the ridgelines and far fewer people on the trail. Either way, this is trekking in some of the most photographed mountains in Japan.

article-392.title: Daisetsuzan Winter Wilderness, Hokkaido
article-392.introtext: Snowshoe and backcountry ski through Hokkaido's largest national park, where volcanic steam rises through some of Japan's deepest, driest powder.
article-392.fulltext:
Daisetsuzan means 'great snowy mountains', and in winter the name earns itself — this is a roadless volcanic massif in central Hokkaido where snow falls dry and deep from December through March, and steam vents still smoke through the drifts on the upper slopes. This trip uses snowshoes and, for stronger skiers, backcountry touring skis to explore terrain far removed from Hokkaido's resort towns.

Base camp is a small onsen ryokan at the edge of the park, with hot-spring baths waiting after every day in the cold. Days are built around snow conditions and weather rather than a fixed script, guided by a local avalanche-trained mountain guide who knows exactly which slopes are safe to explore that morning. This is wild, quiet Hokkaido, not the crowds of Niseko.

article-393.title: Kyoto and Nara: Temples, Gardens and Old Capitals
article-393.introtext: A slow, guided immersion in Japan's two former capitals — thousands of temples, moss gardens, and the deer-filled park at Nara — with time to actually look.
article-393.fulltext:
Kyoto and Nara between them hold well over a hundred UNESCO-listed and nationally protected sites, and most visitors see them in a rushed day trip. This tour instead spends a full week moving slowly between the essential landmarks — Kinkaku-ji's golden reflection, the endless vermillion tunnel of Fushimi Inari, the raked gravel of Ryoan-ji's rock garden — and quieter corners most tours skip, timed early or late to avoid the worst of the crowds.

A day trip to Nara adds Japan's oldest capital, its wooden Todai-ji hall sheltering a 15-metre bronze Buddha, and a park where wild sika deer bow for crackers. Evenings are free to wander Gion's lantern-lit lanes or simply rest at a traditional ryokan. It suits travellers who want cultural depth over a checklist, with a guide who can actually explain what you're looking at.

article-394.title: Seoul to Gyeongju: Korea's Royal Heritage Trail
article-394.introtext: From Seoul's Joseon-dynasty palaces to the Silla royal tombs of Gyeongju, a guided journey through 2,000 years of Korean kingship.
article-394.fulltext:
Korea's history runs deeper than its skylines suggest, and this trip is built to show it — starting in Seoul's Gyeongbokgung Palace, where guards in period dress change formation on the hour, and ending in Gyeongju, once capital of the Silla kingdom and still scattered with grass-covered royal burial mounds rising straight out of the modern town. A high-speed KTX train link makes the transition between the two feel almost too easy.

In between there's Hahoe folk village, hanok tea houses in Bukchon, and Gyeongju's Bulguksa temple and Seokguram grotto, both UNESCO-listed. Evenings in Gyeongju are spent walking among the illuminated tombs and Donggung Palace's lotus pond, lit gold after dark. It's a trip for travellers who want Korea's imperial and Buddhist history laid out clearly, with good food and comfortable hotels throughout.

article-395.title: The Ha Giang Loop: karst mountains and mist by motorbike
article-395.introtext: Ride the hairpin passes of Vietnam's wildest frontier province on the back of an easy rider's bike, through terraced valleys and Hmong market towns.
article-395.fulltext:
The Ha Giang Loop is northern Vietnam's answer to the Andes: a ribbon of switchbacks strung between limestone peaks hard against the Chinese border. This trip puts you on the back of a semi-automatic Minsk or Honda, driven by a local 'easy rider', so you can watch the karst spires of the Dong Van Plateau go by without ever touching the throttle yourself — or take the handlebars for stretches if you'd rather ride solo behind our support jeep. Either way, the road does the work: the Ma Pi Leng Pass, the Nho Que River a thousand feet below, and villages where H'mong, Tay and Lo Lo families still dye cloth with indigo and burn corn liquor in their yards.

Nights are spent in homestays on stilts, sharing rice wine and grilled river fish with your hosts, and mornings start early to beat the mist off the passes. This is not a paved highway tour — expect gravel, weather, and long days in the saddle — but it rewards with some of the most dramatic mountain scenery in Southeast Asia and a version of Vietnam almost no coach tour ever reaches.

article-396.title: Luang Prabang and the Mekong slow boat to the Golden Triangle
article-396.introtext: Wake for the monks' alms procession, wander gilded temples, then drift two unhurried days downriver on a traditional Mekong slow boat.
article-396.fulltext:
Luang Prabang is Laos at its most serene: a UNESCO-listed peninsula of saffron-robed monks, French colonial shopfronts and gold-leafed wats set at the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan rivers. This trip gives the old capital the time it deserves — dawn alms-giving on Sisavangvong Road, the climb up Mount Phousi for sunset, an evening at the night market — before it turns river-bound. From Luang Prabang you board a traditional wooden slow boat and spend two easy days drifting the Mekong to the Golden Triangle, sleeping overnight in the riverside village of Pakbeng, watching water buffalo, fishing weirs and jungle-clad hills slide past at a pace nothing else in the region matches.

It's an unhurried, low-impact way to cross Laos — no long bus rides, no fixed itinerary beyond the current — and it ends at the Thai and Myanmar borders, where the Mekong itself becomes the boundary between three countries. Best suited to travellers who want their days built around a temple bell schedule and a river current rather than an alarm clock.

article-397.title: Flores to Komodo: dragons, phinisi decks and pink-sand bays
article-397.introtext: Sail a traditional wooden phinisi through Komodo National Park, snorkel reef walls and manta cleaning stations, and track dragons on their home islands.
article-397.fulltext:
This is Indonesia's outer-islands trip: three nights and four days living aboard a traditional Bugis-built phinisi schooner, threading between the volcanic islands of Komodo National Park. Days are built around the water — snorkelling coral walls thick with reef fish, drifting over manta ray cleaning stations at Manta Point, swimming Pink Beach where crushed red coral tints the sand — and around the islands themselves, with guided treks on Komodo and Rinca to track the wild dragons that give the park its name, accompanied always by park rangers carrying forked sticks. A sunrise climb up Padar Island, for the three-bay view that's become the park's signature photograph, is a highlight nobody skips.

You sleep on deck under open sky or in simple cabins below, eat fresh-caught fish grilled each evening, and wake to a different bay every morning. It's a physically easy trip — most days are snorkelling and short walks rather than serious hiking — but it demands comfort with basic boat living and a genuine appetite for isolation; some of these anchorages have no other vessel in sight and no phone signal for days.

article-398.title: Palawan island-hopping: El Nido's lagoons to Coron's wrecks
article-398.introtext: Kayak through hidden lagoons walled in limestone, island-hop by outrigger bangka, and snorkel WWII wrecks in the Philippines' most beautiful province.
article-398.fulltext:
Palawan is routinely called the most beautiful island in the world, and this trip is built around the two archipelagos that prove it. In El Nido, traditional bangka boats ferry you between limestone karst islands to the Big and Small Lagoons — paddle a kayak through a narrow cleft in the rock and the water turns an impossible turquoise, walled in on all sides by sheer cliff. Further north, Coron trades lagoons for history: a cluster of Japanese WWII shipwrecks sits in shallow, clear water, accessible to snorkellers as well as divers, alongside Kayangan Lake, consistently ranked among the cleanest bodies of water in Asia.

Travel between the two is by fast passenger ferry along the Bacuit Bay coast, so the trip strings together beach time, boat time and a couple of proper hikes without ever feeling rushed. Expect fresh-grilled seafood on deserted beaches, barefoot afternoons, and a level of water clarity that makes every snorkel stop worth suiting up for.
